MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask leave of the house to move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), the adjournment to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance respecting order in council P.C. 422, dated March 8, 1929, passed under circumstances that amount to an abuse and infringement of the privileges of this house and constituting a serious reflection upon the honour and integrity of the parliament of Canada, and also to discuss the unauthorized and illegal action of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company in proceeding to construct the Beauharnois canal in contravention of the terms of order in council P.C. 422, dated March 8, 1929, and the plans provided therein, and in further contravention of the terms of the British North America Act, the building of the said canal being brought about in such manner as unjustly to deprive the people of Canada of a vast part of the national domain, thus causing a great and irreparable loss unless immediate action is taken by the government in respect thereto.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Speaking on a question of privilege, there is, I believe, in the taking of votes in the house a custom whereby the Assistant Clerk is expected to look first to the Prime Minister on the government side in order amongst other things that the views and wishes of the administration in the matter of recording a vote may be made known. When I saw the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) did not rise when the yeas were called, I assumed that he was taking a view somewhat similar to my own with respect to this matter, namely, that if the matter were one of great importance some notice should have been given in advance of a motion of this kind, so that members *who were interested and who 'had a special knowledge of the matter, might be present. When the Prime Minister did not rise, I assumed that such was his point of view. I could not understand how a matter relating to a transaction of two or three years ago, could just at this moment become one of urgent public importance; I therefore felt that I would join with him in seeking to preserve what I believe to be t'he best procedure under the rules of the house in the matter of debate and governed my actions accordingly. That was the reason why at the outset some of us on this side of the house did not support the motion but conformed to the order in which votes are generally taken in giving our vote only after the other side of the house had recorded its vote.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much the sentiment which the house has expressed in answering the question affirmatively and by such a large majority. It is unfortunate that on a question of this kind, unless you want to throw the whole matter into the purely political arena, you must adopt this method of obtaining a hearing before the house. It would have been quite possible to bring the matter up on a motion to go into supply, but unless you confine the discussion to an amendment to the motion to go into supply you will not have the question you desire to bring up discussed in the manner in which you wish it to be discussed. Furthermore, the government of the day always feels that an amendment on a motion to go into supply is a motion of want of confidence, and therefore I chose this method rather than a motion of want of confidence.
On the 22nd May of last year I asked leave of the house to move the adjournment to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance in connection with the hydro electric development of the Soulanges section of St. Lawrence river. On that occasion I reviewed, more or less inadequately, the history of its development and I hope I succeeded in convincing hon. members that this development was brought about and was being proceeded with in a manner which called for action by the house. The then Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) listened throughout the debate and did not say anything in reply. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), then leader of the opposition, took advantage of that occasion to make some observations, and I shall refer to what the present Prime Minister is reported then to have said. As reported at page 2419 of Hansard of May 22, 1930, the present Prime Minister is reported as saying:
But what position are we in? Tile power that once belonged to Canada and to all the people-and I have a very strong conviction when I use those words-has now passed irrevocably out of our hands. The price at which that power is to be sold for Canadian development is to be passed upon by three managers for the next ten years. That is what it means.
Let us look at this thing fairly. There are the names of the persons concerned; some of them are friends of mine. Does that deter me from the discharge of my public duty here? It does not. My public duty here is to point out just what I am pointing out to this country, that the power development of the great natural resources of power and energy that infuse life into factories and make them efficient instruments for the purpose of making this country great, can come about only by a realization that this development must be under terms and conditions that enable such power to be available to the Canadian people on the cheapest possible terms. These resources are held by us from Providence in trust, not for tihe few but for all; they are held in trust for the Canadian people and not for the few'. I am the last man who would deny to the man wdth enterprise, initiative and courage just compensation for his efforts, but I ask any hon. gentleman sitting opposite, whether he be a capitalist or otherwise, to read the figures given this afternoon and say whether this country of ours has had a fair deal. We are the beneficiaries; the crown in the right of the Dominion has been the trustee; they and they only could grant the permission, and when they granted that permission did they impose a single restriction or condition that would secure to posterity and to this generation as well the use of that great natural power given to us by Providence, the extent and value of which is such that it should make Canada equal any nation in the world?
That is the question. When we talk as we have been talking about the necessity for protection and why it is necessary to put ourselves on terms of even and fair competition w-ith those who are carrying on mass production in other countries, wo must remember that one
Beauharnois-M r. Gardiner

of the most valuable factors, namely, the great hydro-electric possibilities of Canada, is now passing out of our hands and cheap production is then rendered less and less possible. I say, sir, that while I sat in my place and listened, as I did this afternoon for the first time, to those speakers and remembered what I have read as to the' prices at which securities upon the stock exchanges are being sold, I realized that in its possibilities this was one of the most gigantic enterprises this country has ever had to consider, and the question is well worthy of the consideration of parliament even if it were the day before dissolution. I am only sorry that it should not have been considered before this. I have been recreant to my duty in that it has not been so considered and after all I heard during this discussion this afternoon I realized that fact.
I do think, and I say it to the Prime Minister, that this matter should be the subject of judicial inquiry:	It should be inquired into;
there have been statements made which necessitate that procedure being adopted. Why should $3,500,000 be spent for little or nothing? What is the reason for this vast financial scheme? Why, there are now several thousand shares apparently available for sale on the market at $15 per share which, in itself as you will observe, involves a vast sum of money. What is the reason for these things being done without our having some knowledge of just what Mr. Sweezey meant when he pointed out what had to be done in order to secure the results which he has attained?
Go to the United States and watch what they are doing there. We talk about our institutions; the United States Senate lays bare everything. What are we doing in this country? We are pussyfooting about matters of this kind, because men think that your friend or my friend may be associated with this matter, and we have not the courage to stand up and talk about it. Well, sir, I value my position in public life, but I would rather be relegated to private life and be there forever than remain silent on an occasion of this kind.
That is what I have to say; let there be no misunderstanding about it. It may mean that I will be subjected to the threats of the great financial powers that are behind this venture. I snap my fingers: that is my answer.
I confess, Mr. Speaker, when I contemplate this matter and when I regard all that is involved in it, not to thousands but to millions of people who some day will fill this great valley around the St. Lawrence, which might become one of the greatest industrial centres in America-the Ruhr of Canada; when I contemplate what those figures meant this afternoon, my feeling of resentment gets the better of me. I ask hon. gentlemen if this thing is to be tolerated. It rests with us, with each of us, to say whether or not it shall be tolerated, and I believe that in the end the common sense of the Canadian people will prevail and that, great and powerful though the promoters have been, they are not sufficiently powerful to control the common sense of the people of Canada.

I just want to mention now in passing that the Prime Minister was undoubtedly mistaken in saying that "the power has now passed irrevocably out of our hands." I am sure on more mature reflection he will agree with me that that power still belongs to us and not to the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, and that he may still secure for the people of Canada their heritage which Sweezey and his friends are attempting to acquire by fraud and conspiracy.
Hon. members will recall that it was pointed out on May 22 last that the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company first applied to the Dominion government for permission to divert the whole flow of the St. Lawrence river through the Beauharnois canal, beginning with an initial 40,000 cubic feet per second and the approval of its plans to effect such diversion.
This application was so preposterous that the then Liberal government was forced to refuse to entertain it, but only after the most vigorous protests had been made against it. Hon. gentlemen will note that the then Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) in an apparent endeavour to help Mr. Sweezey and his senatorial friends, limited the protests to the question of navigation only, thus preventing any protests being made with respect to other and most important features of this transaction.
Having failed, however, to secure the approval of the original application by which they would get the whole flow of the river, these promoters, with their real object still in view, agreed to amend their application. The application was amended and finally assumed this form:
The application of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company now pending before the governor in council is purely and simply for the approval of plans for hydraulic development which will be subject to a condition that not more than 40,000 cubic feet per second shall be diverted from the river-from lake St. Francis to be returned to lake St. Louis and used for power purposes by the company between these two points: and any condition that the government may exact, in any wording satisfactory to the government, involving that limitation is accepted in advance by the applicant. If the engineers think that the plans should be altered to meet this declaration the company will submit to any such alteration.
It is beyond question that the amended application of the company was for the purpose of securing from the Dominion govern-

Beauharnois-Mr. Gardiner
ment authority to proceed with a hydraulic development which included the right to divert water through the canal the use of this water to produce power, and the approval of the remedial works; the company being specifically limited, however, to a maximum diversion and use of 40,000 cubic feet per second.
The government had no authority to receive or to approve of this application under the powers conferred on it by the Navigable Waters Act or any other act, and of this I am satisfied that some members of the then government should have been aware.
The government in receiving and granting this application conferred on their friends no rights whatsoever. The order in council is illegal because, let me repeat, the government had no authority under the Navigable Waters Act to grant the right to divert and use this water for power development, and the whole Beauharnois development is without real legal foundation and contrary to the laws and treaty obligations of Canada.
But there is another serious aspect to this situation and of immediate interest to the people of Canada as a whole. By one of the terms of the lease of imaginary and wholly non-existent rights which this company secured from the province of Quebec, the company acquired a lease of:
The rights of the province of Quebec to such ' part of the hydraulic powers of the St. Lawrence river that can be developed between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis, through a derivation canal on the right (southern) shore, haying a maximum flowing capacity of 40,000 eubic feet per second, the province reserving the ownership and free disposition of the surplus.
Their lease, size of their canal, the order in council, their plans filed, all absolutely limit them to a diversion of 40,000 cubic feet per second.
Does this lease and the order in council represent the honest and real intentions of those concerned? Was it an honest transaction? What are the real facts? Scarcely had the ink dried on this order in council when these very same promoters proceeded to violate not only the letter but the very spirit of the provincial lease and of the order in council. They prepared plans that provided for the diversion of the whole flow of the river; they sold their bonds on the representation that they would eventually get the whole flow; and they are now building without authority a canal which will take the whole flow, of the river. Further, they have acquired 13,000 cubic feet from the Montreal
Cottons. To add insult to injury, they have secured this past winter 30,000 additional cubic feet from Quebec, and are awaiting a favourable opportunity to ask for another order in council from this government.
It is apparent the then government and these Beauharnois promoters entered into an agreement which they never intended should be carried out. I say the then government was not evidently sincere in limiting the diversion to 40,000 cubic feet, because it is plainly evident from subsequent events that they knew when they imposed this limitation on the company that neither they nor the company ever intended to abide by the terms of this order in council, a single condition of which, designed to protect the people, has not been observed or enforced. Later in the same year a second order in council was passed giving to this company the right to divert this
13,000	cubic feet which they had bought from Montreal Cottons.

speechtext: When?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Late in 1929. I have the evidence under my hand. You see therefore, Mr. Speaker, that when the first order in council was passed it was quite evident that the promoters were not satisfied that they were going to be limited to 40,000 cubic feet. Therefore, when they had an opportunity of securing a further order in council which permitted them to acquire this 13,000 cubic feet, they proceeded to do so, and the government obliged them in that regard. I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that the government of the right hon. the leader of the opposition was unfortunate, in a measure, in somewhat misleading the people of this country in the passing of this order in council, P.C. 422.
The Dominion government and these Beauharnois promoters were either guilty of conspiracy or the government was negligent in respect to the duty it owed to the people of Canada to maintain for the people their possessions and in preventing these from being stolen or illegally acquired by others.
But there are other matters to consider. I ask the Prime Minister, fully believing that he has given this subject serious consideration since May 22 last, if there is any doubt in his mind as to the illegality of the foundation of this whole Beauharnois development from its very inception? And more especially so, as a result of the Montreal Cottons deal and in view of the action of the Quebec government in attempting to grant the company a lease of the power resulting from an additional 30,000 cubic feet which
Beauharnois-Mr. Gardiner

means, coupled with other facts, that the company will continue to secure additional water until the whole St. Lawrence river between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis is dewatered and flows through the Beauharnois canal, or, as the corporation's advertisements say, "forms a new river." I, for one, have no doubts about it.
In addition to this serious phase of the situation we have the amazing spectacle of a number of members of the Senate, all appointed by the former Prime Minister, no doubt in his efforts to reform that august body, identified with this transaction by which they and the other promoters of this enterprise were able to secure possession of the national domain to the nauseating extent of hundreds of millions of dollars, without having one dollar of their own money invested in the enterprise and without giving to the people of Canada one actual dollar's worth of value for the concession. They may say "we are giving the people of Canada a ship canal 600 feet wide, 28 feet deep and 15 miles long." Mr. Speaker, that is an outrageous lie. What deception! An investigation will show that they had to dig this power ditch that size in order to get the necessary quantity of water for their power production; even their literature says so. It was not dug at all, as they and the then government represented, for a navigation canal and given to the people.
If there is any doubt about this deception will the right hon. the Prime Minister and will the right hon. the leader of the opposition explain to the people of this country why it is necessary to have the Beauharnois canal 600 feet wide when the Welland canal which is to form part of the deep seaway is only 310 feet wide? I challenge contradiction and proof thereof, of this statement.
The association of these senators with this enterprise does not make for good government, nor dees it tend to create confidence in the minds of the people of Canada in governmental institutions, and no greater danger confronts us to-day than the loss of such confidence. The circumstances which resulted in these senators becoming identified with this enterprise must be inquired into. Senator McDougald was a member of the national advisory committee on the St. Lawrence waterway. The committee reported to the government on January 11th, 1928. This report was divided in two parts-a majority report and a minority report. Senator McDougald was found among those who subscribed to the majority report. This

is what Senator McDougald, with others, reported and advised the government to do on January 11th, 1928, page 19, paragraph 4:
We believe that the first concern of this committee should be, and of the government will be, the national aspects of the proposed undertaking, and we regard it as most desirable that the initial development take place in the purely domestic section of the river lying within the province of Quebee. We believe that if a reasonable time were permitted in which to enable the resultant power to be economically absorbed the development of this national section would be undertaken by private agencies able and willing to finance the entire work including the necessary canalization, in return for the right to develop the power.
Hon. gentlemen will note the date, January 11, 1928. On April 18, 1928, the Globe and the Mail and Empire published certain articles suggesting, among other things, that Senator McDougald was interested in the Beauharnois Power Company, the Mail and Empire adding a suspicion that Senator McDougald was one of the three men on the advisory committee who advised the government to develop the national section first by private agencies. Senator McDougald felt it necessary to rise in his seat in the Senate on the 19th of April, 1928, and, to use his own language, repel the above implication reflecting on his honour and integrity both as a member of the Senate and as a private citizen. His remarks in respect to the Globe are reported in Hansard as follows:
I want to say here, and to say it with emphasis, that I do not own a dollar's worth of stock in this enterprise, and have no interest in or association with that company in any way, shape or form.
And further:
Speaking for myself, I want to make a further positive and absolute denial of the implications and suspicions of the Mail and Empire. So far as I myself am concerned I cannot add too much emphasis to my denial of the suspicions and aspersions which these despatches have cast upon me as a member of the advisory committee, as a member of this honourable body and as a private citizen. Perhaps I may take some slight comfort from the fact that this sort of thing seems to be one of the ordinary penalties of public life.
The people of Canada to-day are asking if that statement made by Senator McDougald is true. If it is not true, then Senator McDougald deliberately deceived the Senate and the people of Canada. I am simply going to state the facts which are known to the public. Senator McDougald was interested in the promotion of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company in 1927 before the legislative assembly of the prov-

Beauharnoie-Mr. Gardiner
inee of Quebec. The company subsequently, in 1928, again applied for and succeeded in getting a revision of its charter. In 1929 the company came to the Dominion government and succeeded in securing the passage of order in council P.C. 422. In October, 1929, the Beauhamois Corporation Limited purchased from the Beauharnois syndicate the shares of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company. The members of the Beauharnois syndicate received for each unit they held forty shares of the corporation stock and $150 in cash. I have this information before me in a document entitled The Financial Post Survey of Corporation Securities. Senator McDougald received 208,000 Class A common shares and $780,000 in cash from the Beauharnois syndicate for his share in an enterprise which several months previously he had disclaimed any interest in or association with. I have also under my hand documentary evidence as to the allocation of these shares, because I have had the share registers searched, and I have an affidavit under my hand as to the result of the search. He received securities valued, according to their prospectus, at over S30,000,000. That is the statement they make in their prospectus, that the potential value of these 208,000 shares is over $30,000,000.

Senator McDougald is
the chairman of the enterprise. He is also one of the three members who have complete charge of it for the next ten years. What do hon. members think and what will the country think of the facts surrounding Senator McDougald's connection with this enterprise? If it was a reflection on his honour and integrity as a member of the Senate or as a private individual to be suspected of or referred to as being interested in the Beauharnois Company on April 19, 1928, the Canadian people are wondering just * what bearing his present position will have in this respect.
Furthermore, the press despatches carry the startling news that these same gentlemen have been accused of corrupting the administration of justice in the province of Quebec in relation to certain matters in dispute between themselves and another company, in whose affairs I have not the slightest personal interest. A dispute arose between the Beauharnois company and this other company, with the result that a lawsuit was started in the courts in the city of Montreal. As to the outcome of the lawsuit I am, of course, entirely disinterested. But in the course of the proceedings last winter Chief Justice Greenshields-one of whose relatives is identified with the Beauharnois corporation-interfered with the trial, as stated in the press, by withdrawing Mr. Justice Patterson, the trial judge who had started the hearing of the case, and substituting in his place Mr. Justice Boyer.

293. (j) Members are prohibited from casting reflections upon the conduct of judges of superior courts unless such conduct is based upon a substantive motion.

When a member of parliament profits by the exploitation of the public domain, Mr. Speaker, to the extent of approximately $30,000,000, and when this exploitation is only made possible-

I asked the Prime Minister if he would produce the report which he secured last fall ' as a result of the departmental investigation which he ordered. Beauharnois-Mr. Gardiner
close the utter fraud of these promoters in inducing the then government to pass order in council P.C. 422, dated March 8, 1929, because in that order in council the company is limited then and for the future to a canal six arpents or 1,100 feet wide, and this report discloses amongst other evidences of fraud the fact that they are building a canal twenty-one arpents or approximately 4,000 feet wide. 40,000	cubic feet? I am sure the people of this country will feel very much aggrieved.
I have under my hand indisputable evidence that this company acquired from the province of Quebec, the imaginary right to build this 4,000 foot canal on March 20, 3930, over one year after P.C. 422 was passed, and that they are building a canal the plans of which never have been approved, a canal totally and entirely different from the canal referred to in and approved by the order in council. The people of this country are asking and demanding to know all the facts in connection with this Beauharnois development. They are demanding the reason why it was possible for the government of the right hon. leader of the opposition to have granted certain concessions whereby the Beauharnois promoters were able to make such vast and staggering profits out of the public domain. They are demanding to know how it was possible for certain members of the Senate, who are intimate friends of the right hon. leader of the opposition, to acquire the public domain to the extent of tens of millions of dollars, without giving anything in return.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question raised by
the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) is one of great national importance. The St. Lawrence river is more than a river, it is the most important waterway in Canada and one of the most important waterways in the world. The Beauharnois canal enterprise was brought to the attention of this house last year and I made certain observations at that time as to my appreciation of the importance of the matter and of the desirability of the facts being known to the public because of the allegations then made. However, I pointed out that securities had been sold and were in the hands of innocent purchasers. Upon the advent of this government to power and before I went to England I arranged that certain information should be obtained and on my return that information was available. I stated the other day that I did not believe it was in the public interest to bring that information down because it was only what one might term an interim report.

Beauharnois-Mr. Bennett
The St. Lawrence river is undoubtedly being dewatered if the cubic feet per second provided for by the original lease granted to the company by the province of Quebec, plus the leave to take 30,000 second feet additional is given effect to. The river is being dewatered and the water turned into a canal which is not being built as a canal but as a communication between two lakes formerly provided by the river itself.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: That would total 70,000 second feet?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Yes, that would be the
result of the two grants. I have steadily endeavoured, without in any sense being hurried, to secure additional information with respect to the matter. I have been furnished with the opinions of leading counsel that under the Navigable Waters' Protection Act there is power to do certain things and that the jurisdiction of the federal government in the premises is solely as defined by that statute. I have not had time to consider these opinions in detail but when the hon. gentleman says that the canal is larger than was provided for by the order in council issued by the late government he is stating the fact; the engineers' report clearly indicates that.
I deprecate very greatly the references made by my hon. friend to the judiciary. I do not think it serves any useful purpose at this time, although perhaps it may serve one purpose. The government is of the opinion that from the facts which have been stated in this house both last year and this year, an investigation into this matter should take place without delay. I propose to prepare a motion to submit this question either to the consideration of the standing committee on banking and commerce or to a select committee to be appointed by the house. The hon. member may indicate in what terms he would like the order of reference to be made and I promise him that the government will give to his suggestions its closest attention and consideration. The matter is too important even when considered from the standpoint that it only concerns differences between individuals or what profit individuals may or may not make, to be allowed to remain as it now stands. Without anticipating what may be said or making any aspersions upon the good faith or interest of those who have been engaged in the undertaking, we will prepare the necessary motion to submit the matter either to a standing or a select committee of this house.
Mr, E. J. GARLAND (Bow River): Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable pleasure and satisfaction that I have listened to the promise of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). I had felt for some time that the departmental investigation which was undertaken and which he now refers to as an interim investigation was hardly in keeping with the promise made to the house last year of a full judicial inquiry. While we may be satisfied for the time being with an inquiry by a committee of parliament-I understood the right hon. member to suggest a committee of parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I said either a
standing committee or a select committee. Parliament is in session and the observations made this afternoon with respect to the judiciary make it impossible to impose upon any judge of this country a burden which under the statutes he is not required to assume. *

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I am inclined to believe that an investigation by parliament might on the whole be even more satisfactory than a judicial inquiry, although it is quite possible that a judicial inquiry may arise out of the investigation by the committee.
The right hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat referred to the Navigable Waters Protection Act as being the authority under which the order in council was passed which permitted the diverting of these waters by the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company. I submit that there is not a single line, sentence or section in that statute which gave the late government power to divert this water. I have examined the matter somewhat closely, and I find the different events appearing in a regular fashion. The order in council P.C. 422 at the bottom of page 1 refers to the lease granted. This was referred to by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) and reads as follows:
The rights of the province of Quebec to such part of the hydraulic powers of the St. Lawrence river that can be developed between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis through a derivation canal on the right (southern) shore, having a maximum flowing capacity of 40,000 cubic feet per second, the province reserving the ownership and the free disposition of the surplus.
To put it in simpler language, all that this part purported to do was to lease to the company 500,000 horse-power to be developed from the St. Lawrence river between the two lakes which I mentioned. Before that power could be developed, it was necessary for the

1742	COMMONS
Beauharnois-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
company to secure certain other things somewhere else, and so the company came not to parliament, but to the Dominion government and secured the passage of the order in councli to which reference has been made. Let us look at the order in council and find out what they asked for. They asked for the following:
First: approval of the proposed development.
Second: in connection therewith they applied for all such authority from the Dominion government as might be necessary to divert water.
Third: they applied for authority to use an "initial" flow of 40,000 cubic feet per second, pursuant to the provisions of section 5 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
Fourth: the company applied for approval of the plans and site of works to be constructed in the St. Lawrence river with respect to the diversion of the flow of water mentioned above.
Fifth:	After the happening of certain
events and the doing of certain things, the company was to have the right to enlarge its canal and divert through it and utilize for the development of power all the flow of the St. Lawrence river, if their original application had been granted.
All of the original application is embodied in the order in council, and the only alteration that has been made in it is in the amended application which is also in the order in council. The amended application limited the flow to an actual and final flow of 40,000 cubic feet per second. I wonder whether hon. gentlemen realize the implication of that. The company had asked for the right to launch a project for the development eventually of the entire power of the St. Lawrence river. They amended that application, and in the amendment they said in effect: Very well, since the objections have arisen, we shall content ourselves with applying for only 40,000 cubic feet. That is all they got; that is all the order in council purported to give them. As has already been said, they have gone ahead and prepared plans and done actual work for the production of more power than that, but that is aside from this particular point. This amended application was really brought about by the refusal of the late government to grant this company power to divert the whole flow. The company amended their application on representations made. The amended application reads at page 5:
The application of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company now pending before the governor in council is purely and simply 
for the approval of plans for hydraulic development which will be subject to a condition that not more than 40,000 cubic feet per second shall be diverted from the river-from lake St. Francis, to be returned to lake St. Louis, and used for power purposes by the company between these two ponts; and any condition that the government may exact, in any wording satisfactory to the government, involving that limitation, is accepted in advance by the applicant.
In the amended application there is not a word regarding navigation; it deals solely with power.
Therefore we now arrive at this point where we can ascertain and determine what the Dominion government undertook to accomplish by this order in council. We ascertain this:
First: they approved the hydraulic development.
Second: they approved the plans of the company for the proposed hydraulic development.
Third: they assumed the power to grant to the company the right to divert water from the St. Lawrence river through the proposed canal.
Fourth: they attempted to grant to the company the right to divert a total flow of
40,000	cubic feet of water per second from the St. Lawrence through this canal.
Fifth: they approved the plans and site of the company for remedial works that became necessary as a result of such hydraulic development, the remedial works being that part of the development which necessarily had to be constructed in the St. Lawrence river itself.
Sixth: in the amended application, the company applied for the use of a flow of 40,000 cubic feet. That means they asked the Dominion government to grant them the right to the use of 40,000 cubic feet of water for the production of water power.
I assert again that the Navigable Waters Protection Act does not give any government authority to authorize the diversion and use of 40,000 cubic feet or 50,000 cubic feet or any flow from the river.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: It is quite useless without that power.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
The authority to grant this is vested somewhere, but that authority is certainly not vested in the executive council; it is not vested in the government. It is vested, as I shall show in parliament itself, and only by act of parliament could these alleged rights or privileges be extended, because there is no legislative sanction or authority for what has already been done. I

Beauhamois-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
submit that most respectfully. In order to make this clear, let us examine the Navigable Waters Protection Act. "Work" is clearly defined in section 2 whereby work is said to include:
any bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, wharf, dock, pier, or other structure, tunnel or pipe, or telegraph or power cable or wire and the approaches or other works necessary or appurtenant thereto, or any work, structure or device, whether similar in character to the foregoing or not, which may interfere with navigation.
Section 4, which is really the purpose of the act, enacts:
No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site thereof has been approved by the governor in council, nor unless such work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council.
It will be seen that first of all the works are clearly defined. They must be works of such a character that they involve one or both banks of the river. Secondly, they must be in the river or across the river or under the river, or, in short, 'between the two banks of the river. By what stretch of the imagination can it be argued that the act under which this authority is incorrectly claimed, gave the government power to authorize the diversion of water and to sanction the plans for the construction of a development which for its greater part is a long distance from the river? Of course I am not a lawyer and that may be my excuse in this connection, but I cannot understand where one can find in any section of the act any authority whatever for the passing of the order in council. There is no question that the proper authority, as I said a moment ago, is parliament. This whole matter should have come before us as an act of parliament. It should have been dealt with by the house and not by order in council.
In connection with this there are other points that might be taken up. It might be argued, for example, that the government had the right to give sanction to or approve plans for the works. The remedial works only could be involved, and remedial works in this case mean works in the river. Remedial works are not the canal, but this order in council purports to give sanction for plans for the creation of a canal, its curvature, depth, width, breadth and all the rest of it. In my opinion-and I am only a layman-my reading of the act would indicate that the government had no right whatever to approve plans for this canal. They could approve remedial plans in the river itself if such plans wer.e proper to the 22110-nil
undertaking and satisfactorily safeguarded navigation, but that is the limit to which the government could have gone under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. Let us examine that phase of the matter for a moment.
The plans for the remedial works have, in my opinion, and so far as the evidence to my hand goes, never yet been sanctioned. I doubt very much whether the Prime Minister or the Minister of Public Works can inform the house that satisfactory plans for remedial works have ever been placed before the department. They certainly were not sanctioned by the order in council, for the order in council itself points out that the plans already submitted-

No plans of any shape
or form in connection with Beauhamois have been approved by this administration.

I am glad
to hear that. I could hardly understand how an administration that took cognizance of the legal facts in connection with this matter could approve of these plans for remedial works. On page 6 of the order in council I find the following:
With respect to the effect of works on river or rapids navigation-
That is the remedial works:
-the committee

That is, I imagine, the committee of the cabinet:

finds that the diversion of 40,000 cubic feet per second will adversely affect navigation in the Soulanges section and that the works proposed by the company for rectification purposes in this section are not satisfactory.
Could language be clearer? In the order in council itself reference is made to the plans submitted and referred to on page 3 at the bottom of the first paragraph of the present application of the Beauhamois company, these plans consisting of twelve sheets of description. These are the plans to which the order in council refers, and the order in council says that the plans now submitted, and upon which the order in council is presumed to be based, are not of a kind that are satisfactory and that they will not protect navigation. Then it goes further and says:
The committee finds, however, that with modifications therein there is a reasonable likelihood of the present condition being largely recovered. It is pointed out by the committee that these works are largely experimental, are relatively costly, and, in view of the possibility of the balance of power being developed in a short time, the expenditure involved is likely to be lost before many years.

Is the hon. member not

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
All I know is that under the authority of the Navigable Waters' Protection Act the plans approved should have been without question sufficient to protect the navigation rights of the St. Lawrence, but in the order in council itself it is admitted that at the very best, in the opinion of the engineers, it is "'reasonably likely" that the interference with navigation may be "largely recovered." That is the position with respect to the remedial works in the St. Lawrence. As a matter of fact, it may easily be contended that not even the Navigable Waters' Protection Act gives the government power to approve of plans of the character that would be necessary to an enterprise of this kind. Apparently there is no certainty in the minds of the engineers of the department that any remedial works will be satisfactory or that navigation will be fully and properly protected.
I say, then, that the whole basis upon which the Beauharnois development is now being proceeded with is illegal, that it has no foundation or authority in any statute whatever, and that the government had no jurisdiction for passing the order in council; certainly no jurisdiction can be found in my reading of the Navigable Waters' Protection Act, and, under this development, unfortunately, a gigantic alienation of the natural resources of this country to private interests for exploitation is taking place under the monstrous financial scheme that was fully disclosed to the house last year.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Is the argument of the hon. gentleman that the government had no authority by order in council to agree to this diversion because it is not specifically mentioned in the section of the Navigable Waters' Protection Act which my hon. friend read?

Not a soul in this country can say:	Here we have legislative,
statutory or judicial authority stating that we alone own the power. Nobody knows. Why the order in council itself in one of its clauses on page 5 points out:
That in view of the combination of the two questions of power and navigation, it was deemed advisable to refer to the Supreme Court of Canada a series of questions to the end of determining the respective rights of the Dominion and provincial governments in the development of power.

Beauharnois-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
The order in council says:
The supreme court has recently submitted the result of its consideration of the various questions asked. The conclusions of the court do not furnish sufficient ground to establish a ivell-defined line of action with respect to power.
Of course they do not. The whole thing is still undecidied. If hon. gentlemen would turn to clause 21 of the conditions, found on page 10 of the order in council, they will see that it reads:
The approval hereby granted is given upon and subject to the condition that in case it should be judicially determined that His Majesty in the right of the Dominion is entitled to any of the power now or hereafter to be developed in connection with the works the subject of this approval or any works hereafter to be constructed by virtue hereof by the company or which His Majesty may construct then and in such event the company shall pay to His Majesty-
And so on. That clause can be read as meaning many things, but one thing certainly, that it was the intention, implied at least, of the government to make further examination into the ownership of the power. It says here that it is given upon and subject to the condition that in case it should be judicially determined- "in case."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
There is a distinction
between power and water; I should like my hon. friend to keep that in mind.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Yes; in
case it should be judicially determined. In other words, if it be argued that, in order to develop power, it is necessary to grant a diversion of the water, then you have the thing still further confused. The order in council implies that the matter has not been settled by any authority anywhere, and it implies that further examination will be made before the court in respect to ownership. And although the government had themselves, within a few days of that very time, through the Attorney General for the Dominion of Canada argued before the supreme court that the Dominion alone had the right to the power; in spite of the fact that they had prepared an extensive and expensive factum which was signed by many legal authorities, including the former Solicitor General:	in
spite of that fact the Solicitor General of the late administration himself rose in the house, a few days after having contended in the court that the Dominion had the power, and challenging hon. members on this side, argued that the province of Quebec owned the power and should be given authority- a most absurd and ridiculous position to be placed in.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps he was merely
devil's advocate.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
It may be that lawyers lend themselves to that sort of thing; but I submit that in both cases he was speaking or should have been speaking, in the interests of the people of the Dominion. He should have been speaking, first, as their advocate as Attorney General before the Supreme Court of Canada; and, secondly, as a minister of the crown in this house In neither capacity was he representing the interests of Quebec or the point of vie? he held with respect to Quebec; he shoulf have been concerned to preserve, and con tend for, the rights of the people of the wholi Dominion. Does it appear that he was doing so in both cases? One day he argued in th< court to the effect that, "of course, the Dominion has the power; there is nothing to the argument opposing this contention. We own this power; here is the proof." And a few days afterwards he says, "The Dominion has no jurisdiction; it is a matter for the province of Quebec." Well, Mr. Speaker, that is an additional matter that might be investigated.
I do not wish unnecessarily to prolong the debate, Mr. Speaker, because I am more than satisfied with the agreement of the Prime Minister that this whole matter should be sent to a special committee of this house. I do submit however that it certainty is time this be done. If there is one thing that the country is demanding at this time it is that the fullest possible investigation, as full as has been made in the past before a committee of the United States Senate, should be made in regard to power matters in Canada. I say without fear of contradiction, that the gigantic control, on the part of small groups of powerful financiers, of these immensely valuable natural resources upon which, as the Prime Minister said last year, the life, the welfare, the happiness and wellbeing of millions of people in the future depend-the right hon. member used words to that effect, I believe-is a matter of the gravest concern to the people of this Dominion. And any alienation of these resources to private interests by order in council must be investigated; we must look into such questions as cost of production of power and the prices charged the consumer. In my opinion the time is coming when, if necessary, amendments to the British North America Act must be secured in order to give this government authority to preserve the rights of the consuming public in this country. I say therefore that the narrower
1746	COMMONS
Beauharnois-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
and narrower, the smaller and smaller these groups become-such financial groups as the Sweezey and the Holt concerns who are now more and more controlling this great resource -the more certain is it that we must by legislative interference' on the part of the Dominion of Canada protect the rights of the consuming public of the country.
It has been suggested that as third parties are now involved by the purchase of the bonds and shares certain vested rights have been created and therefore nothing can be done in connection with the matter. Let me however point out that under section 12 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, under which the whole thing is purported to have been made possible, parliament may take action. Let me quote from the act:
Parliament may, at any time, annul or vary any order of the governor in council made under this part.
Therefore, if it be found that the inferences I have drawn from the facts as I have set them out are correct, that this government had no legal authority for the order in council, and that the plans have not been ratified nor sanctioned-because no plans suitable to enterprises of this character could yet have been before the Department of Public Works then I say that the whole basis upon which this development has taken place is illegal and the agreement should be cancelled forthwith.
Then comes the point-1 suggested a moment ago, namely, the question of third party interests. We did not worry about the third party interests in the form of the taxpayers of Canada when we abandoned development at Port Nelson upon the recommendation of Mr. Palmer. The former Minister of Railways advised, and the house agreed, that the development at Nelson should be abandoned, and Fort Churchill was decided upon instead -properly and wisely in my opinion. But that involved the loss of 16,242,000 of money expended at Port Nelson. It was profitable and wise to take this course, and I venture to say it would be found profitable and wise in this instance to forget the third party interests involved especially as this Dominion is not concerned in any way, by law or otherwise, in the matter. The stock and bonds of the corporation were disposed of to certain associates of Mr. Sweezey and others through their companies, the Dominion Securities Corporation and Newman Sweezey and Company. These companies in turn sold to the public. The issue is therefore as between the public and these bond companies, not as between the public and the Do'minion, nor between the public and the provinces, unless fMr. E. J. Gariand.]
it be found that fraud has been perpetrated on the public. In that event these associates of Mr. Sweezey, and Mr. Sweezey himself, should be assailed in the courts and made to pay over the necessary amount to make good their exploitations.
If I had time, Mr. Speaker, I would direct the attention of the house to other illustrations to bear out my contention in this regard. I have in my hand the examination which was made by the Commission of Conservation of Canada with regard to Long Sault rapids, and development in connection therewith, in the St. Lawrence. Hon. gentlemen will recollect that in that case the development involved a tremendous amount of public money, and the whole project was cancelled by law. It happened in the United States, in the state of New York-not in this country- but it is an illustration of the wise action taken to protect the whole public interest even though at the sacrifice of a few investors. I certainly hope therefore that investigation before a committee of this house of the question now before us will be as full as possible.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman knows that he must not impute motives to any hon. member.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I was not imputing motives, I was judging the situation in the light of what has taken place to-day, and I said if what the hon. member for Acadia had primarily in mind was a full and thorough discussion of this subject on the floor of the house to-day, we would not have been precipitated into this debate without acknowledge in advance of bis intention to bring this matter up. Let me say at once that I for one am more than delighted that the Prime Minister has undertaken to grant a committee of investigation into this matter, because some of these hon. gentlemen in the far corner will then get a chance to make good some of the general statements and reflections that they have been making on the floor of the house about judges, members of parliament, and everyone else who does not happen to be one of their number.
With respect to the so-oalled Beauharnois project, it is advisable that it should be made perfectly clear to the house and to the country just what the relation of the federal government to this matter has been and is. As I have already said, I must ask the indulgence of the house in speaking without having had an opportunity of looking at any of the past records. I do not wish to be held too closely to technical exactness in what I am about to say. Broadly speaking, the outstanding facts, as I understand them, are these. The St. Lawrence river is, having regard to the territory through which it flows, in part, an international waterway; in part, a national waterway exclusively in the province of Quebec or in a part of the adjoining province. Where the St. Lawrence river is exclusively in

the province of Quebec this parliament has not jurisdiction over the power rights or any other matters affecting the water, except in so far as there is imposed on it the obligation of safeguarding navigation under the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
May I go a step further? In order to incorporate a company such as the Beauharnois Light. Heat and Power Company, it is essential that a charter shall be obtained from the government of the province, not from the government of the Dominion. This government has given no charter to the Beauharnois company respecting power rights, nor has this parliament or any federal government given any right to the Beauharnois company with respect to power rights. Those rights have been obtained from the government of the province of Quebec. If they have been illegally obtained, or if there are matters that are not as they should be with respect to any phases of the transaction, the place in which those matters should be discussed is on the floor of the legislature of the province of Quebec and not on the floor of this parliament, though I have no objection to this parliament taking up its time with provincial mlatters if, even indirectly, they can be shown to have a bearing in so far as federal matters are concerned.
Mr. LaVERGNE: The St. Lawrence is not a provincial matter.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: No, the St, Lawrence is not a provincial matter, but the St. Lawrence in the province of Quebec is regarded by that province as being within its jurisdiction so far as the granting of power rights are concerned, and those rights have been granted by the province of Quebec to this company. If the government of the province of Quebec had no authority to grant those rights then surely, under the laws of the land, there are methods of restraining the government in that particular and of preventing the granting of those rights.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE

Mr. MACKENZIE KING.* If I were an expert in the law and had been paying special attention to this phase of the question, I could answer my hon. friend offhand, but I must say to him at the moment that he will have to accept the statement, as I think he will be prepared to accept it, that if a province does a thing which it has no right to do, then under the laws of this country there are methods at law whereby the province can be restrained.

speechtext: And if the Dominion government does something it has no right to do?

speechtext:
Yes, and I am glad my hon. friend has now brought the matter to a head. The function of the Dominion is to pass upon any power rights or diversions of water granted by provinces with respect to their not interfering with navigation. I will read the clause under which the Dominion has authority in these matters:
No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site thereof has been approved by the governor in council, nor unless such work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council.
That is the extent of the functions and duties of the federal government and of this parliament with respect to such matters as power rights and diversions of water on the St. Lawrence in connection with a company such as the Beauharnois company. The plans are submitted to the government; they are then submitted by the government to its engineers and on the technical advice which is given to the administration it acts in granting approval of those plans. Bu't its function is confined to the approving of plans. That is what was done by order in council, and the statute says that the approval is to be given by order in council. It makes that quite clear. The government in proceeding by order in council is not usurping the functions of parliament. Parliament passed this act; parliament gave to the government or placed upon the government of the day the responsibility of approving of plans by that
method, by order in council. To listen to hon. gentlemen who have spoken one would think that because the government of the day passed some order in council instead of getting an act of parliament, they had been going behind parliament in order to confer some special powers or favours upon political friends

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: At this point I shoulc like to ask a question. Does the act give the government power to divert water?

speechtext:
I think I have made clear what the powers of the federal government are and what is the method of procedure. In all this matter the action of the government has been entirely regular Now let me read this further section, and I will ask my hon. friends who have spoken to pay particular attention:
Parliament may, at any time, annul or vary any order of the governor in council made under this part.
In other words, this order in council was passed, so far as the federal government functions in the matter, over two years ago; it was passed in March, 1929. For two years hon. members who have spoken to-day have had the right to introduce in this house a motion which would annul that order in council, and this parliament had full authority to annul it. All they had to do was to make out a case before parliament why the order in council should be annulled. They have not done that, but they have come here and have made insinuations against pretty nearly every person other than those who belong to their own particular group, as if no one in this world possessed aught in the way of integrity except themselves. I wish to say to one or two of my hon. friends in the far corner that the public will believe that hon. members of the old political parties in this country have just as .fine a sense of honour and just as high a sense of integrity as members of any group in this house who may not happen to belong to one or other of those two parties. It ill behooves them, when there is a statute which was passed by parliament expressly to provide a means of dealing in a parliamentary way with a matter such as this, and when they have not availed themselves of that means, to come and make insinuations of the general character which we have had this afternoon.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that is perhaps about all it is necessary to say at this time. I hope I have made clear first of all that so far as the Beauharnois company is concerned,.
1750	COMMONS
Bcauharnois-Mr. Mackenzie King
it is a company which obtained its charter from the government of the province of Quebec. It obtained whatever rights it has with respect to power from the government of Quebec and obtained whatever rights it has with respect to diversion from the same government. As far as the government of Canada, whether under the old administration or the present administration, is concerned, it had nothing to do with this matter except to approve of those plans from the. point of view of the protection of navigation. If there has not been the protection of navigation on the St. Lawrence in the approval granted that there should be, then certainly the administration which granted the approval without sufficiently safeguarding navigation should be criticized and taken to task in the matter. My hon. friend said this afternoon, "Why is it that you have made the canal twice as wide in Quebec as you have made the Welland canal?"	My
answer is that we wished to be doubly sure that the rights of navigation would be fully protected in that part of the St. Lawrence river. That is the answer to that question. There were no ulterior motives of the character which have been insinuated here this afternoon. That is the position, and may I say that I believe the public of this country, as well as hon. members of this house, will be more' than gratified when this matter of the Beauharnois development and anything that can be brought up incidental to it is finally referred to a committee. There everyone will be given a chance to prove any charge he may bring, but he will be obliged to prove it not by insinuation under the privilege which he has as a member of parliament, but by evidence of a character which would be accepted in a court of law.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE

Mr. Speaker, in view of the
very satisfactory statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) I had hesitated to continue this discussion, but now that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has spoken, all my hesitation has vanished. He worked himself up into a righteous indignation with regard to the methods adopted by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner), which may or may not have been quite correct; but that is not what we are concerned with to-day. We are concerned with certain facts which we wish to lay before the house. It was only by a very narrow margin, that we were able this afternoon to bring this question before the house, and so it seems to me that we should not let slip this opportunity of informing the

general public with regard to the whole situation.
I do not think the public of Canada are informed either as to the facts or as to the great issues at stake. It might well be said that the committee which has been promised will discuss the details of this matter, but on the other hand I would like to call attention to the fact that the corporation has been carrying on a very extensive and persistent publicity campaign across Canada ever since this matter was taken up a year ago. The leader of the opposition seemed to be rather surprised that the matter should come up before the house this year. In view of the charges which were made last year, and of the definite statement of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) that he would bring the matter up again, I cannot quite understand why the right hon. member did not understand that it would be taken up again. Hon. members have received resolutions and letters in regard to it, and it would seem to me to be a matter of course that this question should be brought up for further discussion. The one thing I did not like in the statement of the Prime Minister was the suggestion that because securities had been sold there might be some difficulty in regard to cancellation. I think that was the idea in his mind.
