speechtext:
If that is the law
then there should be some decided amendments, because the rights of the people should be protected. If a corporation is required only to issue a few bonds and manages in some illegal way to get its pro-

Beauharnois-Mr. Wooilsworth
position before the public in order to be secured, it is time the country knew about it and had the necessary amendments passed. With the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) I see no reason why an annulment should not take place.
In view of what the leader of the opposition has said I should like to state my interest in this matter. I believe first of all in public ownership; that is one of my prime interests in this question. The recent administration alienated the Seven Sisters falls in spite of the protests made. I have never been convinced-

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: That was Taschereau power.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I do not want to
get into Quebec, I am in Manitoba at the present moment. The Seven Sisters falls should have remained the property of the people for the use of the people. I would direct the attention of this house to the fact that already the Insull interests have acquired a large part of the stock of the Winnipeg Electric interests. I think it is an outrage thus to alienate the patrimony which we have inherited, and turn it over to American interests.
Further, I am firmly convinced that the Beauharnois corporation is not legally entitled to the power in the St. Lawrence. That being the case it seems to me that as a public man I have to do everything in my power to call attention to the situation.
It has been suggested by the leader of the opposition that there was something sinister in the fact that certain hon. members have been working on this power proposition. I will say very frankly, that I have been furnished with information by interested parties on both sides, as have, I presume, nearly all hon. members. In relation to almost every important question which comes before the house it is a common thing for us to obtain memoranda from the various parties interested. I have no hesitation in saying that I have received information in this case. I did not use any of these memoranda or documents without carefully considering them and making them my own.
It has been said that those who are opposing the actions of the corporation now in control are playing the game of a rival corporation. There is always a danger of that, but I want to state that I will be the first to protest against any irregular procedure on the part of any other corporation. I have no particular antagonism to the Beauharnois Company as such, but I protest against the irregularities connected with their obtaining this power.
Whether or not power in Quebec is Taschereau power, private power or public power,
I need not argue. I maintain that the water powers in the St. Lawrence river should be under public control and if possible under public ownership. Let me direct attention to some of the legal aspects of this case. The other evening we were discussing the British North America Act and at that time, as in the past, we heard a great deal about provincial rights. I should like to take a few minutes to talk about Dominion rights, a matter about which we hear very little, although I acknowledge that we did hear something of this the other day from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie).
The claims of the Beauharnois Power Corporation are based on the original rights of the Roberts. The present undertaking is simply an extension of earlier works. If any hon. member has any doubt in regard to this matter I would refer him to the Exchequer Court Reports, volume IX The judgment appearing there gives an outline of the history of the Beauharnois power proposition. I think I will take about five minutes of my time to summarize that history.
The history of the Beauharnois begins with the Marquis of Beauharnois, owner of the seigneurv of the county of Beauharnois which he acquired from King Louis of France. The marquis or his descendants erected a feeder running from lake St. Francis to the river St. Louis and drew water from lake St. Francis through the feeder for the purpose of developing power at Beauharnois to operate a mill which belonged to them. This feeder or canal was constructed early in the last century by the then seigneur of Beauharnois, through his own lands for the purpose above indicated, and from that time to the present, he and his grantees have continued to use the water supplied by the feeder for the purposes mentioned. Later in the century when the Beauharnois canal was constructed by the government of Canada it was found that it had the effect of raising the water along the south shore of lake St. Francis. To overcome this difficulty a dyke was constructed, the contract being dated March 1, 1855. This dyke crossed the feeder. The gates at the head of the feeder which the seigneur had built were removed when the dyke was constructed and replaced by gates constructed as part of the public works and which formed part of the dyke. Title was acquired in some way by the crown to the land upon which the dyke and the gates were built. This dyke and the gates were the property of the late
Beauharnois-Mr. Woodsworth

province of Canada, the title of which passed to the Dominion in 1867 by the British North America Act. After the construction of this dyke and head gates the seigneur remained in possession of the feeder and in disposing from time to time of mill properties on the St. Louis river, of which he was the owner, he granted to the purchasers a right to the use of the waters supplied by the feeder. This condition of affairs continued until 1882 or 1883 when the Dominion government took possession of the head gates and feeder as well as the St. Lawrence river, and made improvements on the river, deepened and improved the feeder, constructed a bridge over it and took out and rebuilt the head gates.
The Dominion government remained in possession until 1888. In that year some arrangement was arrived at between the late J. B. Robert and the government whereby he was given the keys to the head gates and allowed the use of the feeder until 1892. In the meantime he had acquired practically all the rights of mill owners in the vicinity of the feeder of the river St. Louis. In February, 1892, the government resumed possession of the feeder and control of the head gates against the will and consent of Robert who gave up the keys of the gates to avoid difficulty but without waiving any of his rights. This condition of affairs continued until 1904 when an action was brought by the Roberts against the government for possession of the head gates and feeder. This action was tried in the exchequer court and decided against the Roberts. Negotiations continued until 1909 when an agreement was reached whereby the government passed an order in council authorizing the minister of public works to lease to the Roberts the head gates, feeder and the use of the water to be diverted to the feeder for the production of power at and for the sum of one dollar per year.
In 1902 the Roberts incorporated the Beauharnois Light, Heat & Power Company, to which they transferred certain of their rights. In 1910 the agreement with the government referred to was assigned to this company, which has continued to lease the head gates, the feeder and the water, paying to the government the agreed rental. This condition of affairs has continued up to the present time.
I have summarized that statement from the judgment in order that the house may have something of a background, and also to reinforce my statement that to-day all the extensions that have been made and the powers claimed go back to the original rights of the Roberts. That is dearly recognized from
TMt. Woodsworth.!
the fact that the present corporation is paying a rental to the Dominion government. I think this letter might be of interest:
Newman, Sweezey and Company Limited, Investment Brokers,
136 St. James Street,
Montreal,
29th October, 1927.
Your file No. 804-1 B
The Deputy Minister,
Department of Public Works,
Ottawa, Out.
Dear Sir:
We enclose herewith our cheque for one dollar ($1) in payment of the annual rental due by Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, as assignees of the interests of the lessees, in an agreement dated December 29, 1909, between His Majesty the King and Dame Sarah Roberts et al.
This agreement was assigned to Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company by deed of transfer dated March 26, 1910-authentic copy of which was filed with your department on June 27, 1927, and acknowledged by the secretary of vour department under date of June 29. 1927-file No. 804-1-B.
Will you please acknowledge receipt of this rental in due course.
Yours faithfully,
Hugh G. Griffith.
There was a similar letter dated October 20,
1928,	another similar one dated October 17,
1929,	and then I have here a copy of a receipt from S. E. O'Brien. These documents indicate that the ownership and control of the St. Louis river feeder by the Dominion government were clearly recognized; otherwise why was this annual rental paid?
Not only is this the case with regard to this particular work and feeder on the St. Lawrence, but there are certain other public works that are distinctly the property of the Dominion. The hon. member for Bow River referred incidentally to the factum on behalf of the Attorney General of Canada in the Supreme Court of Canada. This factum is the case of the Dominion government as argued before the Supreme Court of Canada:
In the matter of a reference as to the relative rights of the Dominion and the provinces, respectively, in relation to the proprietary interest in, and legislative control over, waters with respect to navigation and water-powers created or made available by or in connection with works for the improvement of navigation.
The factum is dated 1928. On page 67 of this factum we observe that "all those portions of the St. Lawrence navigation, from Kingston to the port of Montreal, improved at the expense of the province," were vested in the crown and eventually became the property of the Dominion by virtue of the British North America Act of 1867.

Beauhamois-Mr. Woodsworth
The leader of the opposition is trying to evade the issue by making the Beauhamois development a purely provincial matter. It is not in any sense a provincial matter. Under the British North America Act of 1867 t/his was one of the properties that distinctly became the property of the Dominion of Canada. Since the leader of the opposition wants to throw discredit on those of us who are taking up this matter-although I do not know why he should-I think I had better read from the factum itself. On page 67 I find:
94. By section 108 of the British North America Act, 1867 (App. p. 83, lines 32-33) the public works and property of each province enumerated in the third schedule (App. p. 85, lines 21-22) to this act were declared to be the property of Canada. The third schedule enumerates, under the caption "provincial public works and property to be the property of Canada," the following amongst others.
This can be found in the British North America Act, a copy of which I hold in my hand.
X. Canals, with lands and water-powers connected therewith.
This is the statement of the Dominion government itself that the powers in the St. Lawrence enumerated here belong to the Dominion government?
Mr. LaVERGNE:	Who represented the
Dominion government?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I think the hon.
member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) mentioned one of the representatives: the former Solicitor General. This, however, is the statement, and while I am not always quite sure with regard to my legal grounds, I fancy this presentation as put forward by the Dominion government stands until in some way it has been overturned by legal decision, and that has never taken place. This then is the position of the Dominion government itself. Under and by virtue of section 108 of the British North America Act and the third schedule, this canal and the water powers connected therewith, passed to the Dominion government in 1867, and having so passed, they still belong to the Dominion government. Thus as a matter of fact, Quebec has no jurisdiction whatever.
Let me go a step further. In the lease of this corporation,' the province claims the right to all the water powers. I would refer the house to order in council P.C. 422, in which these words are used:
The province reserving the ownership and free disposition of the surplus.
I would point out that in addition to the Beauhamois Light, Heat and Power Company which is still paying a rental to the Dominion government, we have the Dominion government leasing part of the hydraulic power in the St. Lawrence river between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis to the Montreal Cotton Company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Acquired by Beauharnois.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Yes, but my point is this: that the lease is given by the Dominion government; it is not a provincial matter, although in some curious way, I am informed that the province is receiving a sort of second rental for this. I do not know how they have the right to do this, but the province itself is charging a rental.
Another corporation, the Canadian Light and Power Company, has leased power from the Dominion government, and there is also a possibility that the Cedar Rapids Power and Manufacturing Company, one of the other companies in this district, has also leased power from the Dominion. I would refer to the factum at page 105.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: There is a condition in the lease that the Beauhamois would have to pay any damages that would accrue with respect to Cedar Rapids.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and there have been some cases of compensation with regard to this matter. My submission is that if the Dominion owns part of the hydraulic powers of the St. Lawrence river, the exclusive claims of the province are untenable. Indeed, the presumption is that the Dominion government is the agency which has legal authority and right to lease this power.
At this stage in some way or another, Quebec comes on the scene-I say advisedly, "in some way or another," because I do not know how it was managed.
Mr. LaVERGNE :	Behind the scenes.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps behind the scenes, as my hon. friend suggests. But in any case, in the act of incorporation of 1902 of the Beauhamois Company, they were given the right to build a canal 120 feet wide between this feeder and the river St Louis, and in 1910 the act of incorporation was amended to allow the company to build a canal of six arpents or 1,100 feet wide. In 1928 the act of incorporation was further amended allowing them to change the location of the intake on lake St. Francis and the position of the outlet from river St. Louis to lake St. Louis. In 1930, when the

Beauharnois-Mr. Woodsworth
securities were already in the hands of the public, further amendments were secured, allowing the company to widen the canal to 4,000 feet.
Let me point out again that the enlargements and extensions are based on the original rights of the Roberts. There is no other basis. That was the position taken by Mr. Geoffrion in seeking the amendments in 1928. I have his statement here, but have not time to read it; as I understand it, however, the whole claim was based essentially on the original rights of the Roberts.
Let me pass to another phase of this question, in which I think we shall see that the province has also exceeded its jurisdiction. By subsection 11 of section 92 of the British North America Act the province is permitted to incorporate companies with provincial objects only. That is as far as the power of the province goes. If a company's works and undertakings are of such a character as to extend actually or potentially beyond the limits of a province, they are manifestly not provincial objects for the establishment, control and operation of which a provincial company can be incorporated. Again, Mr. Speaker, I am drawing my statement from the factum itself.
The Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company was incorporated by the legislature of the province of Quebec, chapter 72 of 2 Edward VII, 1902. Section 12 of the act incorporating the company gives the company the right to supply, sell and distribute light, heat and power in any direction within a radius of thirty miles of the town of Beauharnois. By a later amendment, that radius was extened to within forty miles from the town of Beauharnois, within which the company may supply, sell and distribute light, heat and power. As a matter of fact, while these I suppose are more or less standard clauses, before you come to the limit of thirty or forty miles from Beauharnois you come to the boundary of the province of Ontario and to the international boundary. It was the evident purpose of the company to distribute power in Ontario, or possibly in the United States; that is, the company was permitted to transmit electricity within this radius, which contemplates the erection by the company of transmission wires entering the United States or the province of Ontario or connecting with transmission wires at the boundary. That was the object of the company. Let me read again from the factum:
Where the objects of a company fall within section 92 No. 10 (a) it is clear that the [Mr Woodsworth.]
Dominion has exclusive legislative power to incorporate such company and grant it all powers required for the construction and operation of the proposed work, including, inter alia, the power of expropriation.
I am not going into the rather technical details which are contained in the factum. But I would urge that the act of incorporation is ultra vires, since the company's objects were not local or provincial but rather interprovincial.
I mighlt go on to show that not only had we the original company, but this company formed a sort of subsidiary known as the Beauharnois Transmission Company, evidently for the purpose of taking electricity from the point of production and distributing it throughout the territory served by the company.
The company was formed by a Quebec charter, and inasmuch as these wires go outside the province and are evidently designed to carry on works outside the province, I urge thait this company also becomes a company having interprovincial objects. It is clear that the Dominion government alone has the exclusive authority and jurisdiction to incorporate a company to undertake a development such as is now being undertaken by the Beauharnois Light, Heat & Power Company.
But I come to an even more important consideration than that, and one which some of us emphasized last year, namely that the whole St. Lawrence scheme is essentially a Dominion project. It ought never to be considered a merely local matter; in fact, that situation is more or less recognized by the Beauharnois company itself,' because in its prospectus issued on December 8, 1930, it says:
In providing deep water navigation in its power canal, the Beauharnois Power Corporation is providing one of the major links in the deep waterways by canalizing all the wholly-Canadian section of the river, save for the stretch around the Laehine rapids at Montreal.
We all know that the St. Lawrence system extends all the way from the head of the great lakes right through to the sea; and here is one of the major links, acknowledged as such by the corporation itself, and yet we are going to allow it to go into the hands of a private corporation. I think it is absolutely absurd. We have spent I do not know how many tens or it may be hundreds of millions of dollars in the Welland canal, and yet the whole of that important project may be rendered useless if we allow the control of Beauharnois to pass to a private corporation.
Mr. LaVERGNE: They could stop navigation in a day if they wanted to.

Beauhamois

Mr. Woodsworth

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Yes, that is true, and a friend of mine, Mr. R. K. Finlayson, a good Conservative in politics, wrote a letter not long ago to the Manitoba Free Press, urging that we can do that and should do that. We can plug the canal, but I fancy that there are vested interests at stake which, if they can prevent us from annulling the lease, would protest vociferously if the government undertook to plug the canal.
Mr. LaVERGNE: I say that the company could stop navigation.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I misunderstood my hon. friend. I suppose they could, although navigation is supposed to be protected by the order in council. May I here read a statement from the factum that I could not find a moment ago when I was dealing with the limitations of provincial companies. At page 108:
It 13 now well established that it is the potential scope of the authorized objects and not the area of their actual exercise or operation which determines the character of the work or undertaking as being federal, and where the authority conferred covers works or undertakings which may extend beyond the limits of a province, such works or undertakings are therefore non-local and fall to the exclusive jurisdiction of the Dominion by virtue of section 92, 10 (a) of the British North America Act.
But, Mr. Speaker, this is not simply a question as between the provincial authorities and the federal authorities. It is not simply an interprovincial question, but an international matter as well. I submit that the works contemplated by the Beauharnois development are of such a class as to bring them within the jurisdiction of the Treaty of Washington of 1871, or the Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909, or within a treaty to be entered into between Canada and the United States with respect to the St. Lawrence deep seaway. Being works of such a nature, they would be subject to the exclusive legislative control of the Dominion. That, too, is clearly substantiated by the argument as contained in the factum at page 95:
Article 3 (App. p. 50), further provides that, except as provided elsewhere by the treaty or by special agreement, no further or other uses or obstructions or diversions, whether temporary or permanent, of boundary waters . . . should be made.
At page 97 of the factum certain fundamental principles are laid down. I quote:
The Attorney General submits that the Dominion has the exclusive legislative control over water-powers created or made available by the works referred to in this question, for the
following reasons:	The parliament and government of Canada alone are empowered under the British North America Act to carry out and perform the obligations of Canada under such a treaty.
In order that Canada should obey the spirit as well as the letter of the various treaties which have hitherto been entered into between Great Britain and Canada, on the one hand and the United States, on the other, and in order that we may 'be free with regard to the proposed treaty between the United States and ourselves, parliament should at once annul the lease which has been granted to the Beauharnois corporation by order in council.
There is another matter which I must touch upon, however briefly, and which I regard as of very great importance, and that is the fact that the order in council goes directly in face of the advice of the joint board of engineers, whose recommendation is against such a scheme as is proposed by the Beauharnois people.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	Why?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I too should like
to ask, why it is that the late government went directly in face of the advice of their own engineers. That question has never been answered. And again let me say to the leader of the opposition, if he is in the house, that we are not taking our cue merely from some people who happen to have personal interests. This action in disregard of the engineers' report is dealt with in the articles to which I have referred and which may be elaborated later in the discussion- I hope they will-as published in the Manitoba Free Press, one of the leading organs of public opinion and one that has generally supported the late government.
We had several years ago considerable trouble with regard to the Chicago drainage canal, and we protested very vigorously against the waters there being diverted for United States purposes, even though they were for sanitary purposes; and if you will look at the factum you will find a certain order under which the waters may be diverted'. But we must admit that the United States government during the last, ten years has consistently refused to grant any rights on the international section of the river. Canada should do at least as much. We have hopes of some day having a deep waterway scheme realized, and it does seem to me that by this action the late government has impaired the success of that scheme. And,

Beauharnois-Mr. Woodsworth
incidentally, it has not lived up to the treaties or the understandings which existed between Canada and the United States.
Let me now summarize, in closing, the paints I have tried to make. The claims of this corporation are based essentially on the old claims of the Roberts. The Dominion government owns the Roberts' works, as is shown by the fact that the present corporation is paying a nominal rental charge to the Dominion government. Under the British North America Act, public works on the list. Lawrence were definitely put under Dominion jurisdiction. There is no doubt about that-If any hon. member questions it, I would advise him to read the British North America Act. Further than that, provincial claims to water-power have apparently no foundation; I have never seen any ground on which these claims are based. Moreover, the province can incorporate only such companies as contemplate distinctively provincial objects-and the objects of the Beauharnois corporation are decidedly not provincial but, in fact, interprovincial in character. The St. Lawrence system is essentially a great Dominion project, and if we are ever to carry it through successfully we cannot allow anything to stand in the way. Finally, this whole question involves our international obligations.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the whole matter should be given the most careful consideration, and I should like to think that some of us at least may be free from any imputation that we are personally interested. There are some people who have stock in Beauharnois. There are some people who have bought the corporation's bonds. There are some people who hope to get something out of it. And there are some who perhaps hope to get something out of those who are opposed to Beauharnois. But some of us are in the happy position of being able to declare that we do not hope to get a red cent out of the business. We feel that it is in the interests of the public as a whole that this question be brought into the full light of publicity and that, if it is at all possible, this great waterway, with the enormous potential water-powers which it carries, shall be saved for coming generations in Canada.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	Was there any excuse
for the order in council?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I think it was very clearly shown by the hon. member for Bow River that the late government quite exceeded its powers as granted under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. Perhaps it
(Mr. Woodsworth.]
might be well for me to put on record one pertinent section. Section 4 reads:
No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site thereof has been approved by the governor in council, nor unless such work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council.
This appears in chapter 140 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1027, section 4. There have been no such plans made and approved, and certainly the operations that are now being carried on by the Beauharnois people have not received any sanction, even by order in council from the late government. Nor, as we have been informed to-day, have they received any sanction from the present government. So that undoubtedly the recent government went entirely outside the terms of this act when it granted the lease.
Mr. LaVERGNE: Why?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
The question is
asked, why? I am not so much concerned why they did it; that might bring the discussion into the realm of imputation, and to-day I have made no imputation. I have confined myself to what I consider to be the facts, and for the most part I have read from the official documents concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I desire, with the consent of the house, to lay on the table certain correspondence that has taken place between the State Department of the United States of America and the Department of External Affairs of the Dominion of Canada. It deals with commuters, and consists of a note from the Canadian Legation to the State Department on December 20th, an acknowledgment from the State Department of December 30th, and the full reply dated May 11th.
The main provision in the reply of the Secretary of State is that commuters who have been properly admitted as immigrants under general order No. 86 will be accorded the same consideration as if they had actually taken up their residence in the United States. It is further implied that loss of employment

Caughnawaga Bridge
in the United States by aliens of the immigrant commuter class of less than six months will not involve abandonment of status. It is provided that commuters who visit European countries without securing reentry permit or a new immigration vise on their return will be assumed to have abandoned their status, inasmuch as one of these documents is required of an alien resident in the United State to secure reentry. The information as to procedure in the latter part of the Secretary of State's note indicates certain concessions from the usual practice to facilitate reconsideration of the cases of persons already rejected. The final paragraph of the note permits persons rejected as commuters to apply for temporary entry to the United States as visitors, and constitutes a general exception to the regulation that persons who have been rejected may not be admitted to the United States within one year except by special permission of the Secretary of Labour.
I lay two copies of the correspondence on the table.

speechtext:
This bill, I believe, is similar to the bill introduced near the close of the last session of the last parliament. At the time my right hon. friend the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), who was then leading the opposition, took exception to ithe bill on the score that it necessitated payment of tolls. On section 1-Auditors not to be directors or officers.

It seems to me the proviso is a little cumbersome and probably does not quite effect the object the promoter of the bill has in mind. I would suggest, and move

Companies Act-Auditors
accordingly, that the proviso be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
Provided however, that the subsection shall not apply to any private company, nor to any company whose shares, bonds, debentures or debenture stock are not offered for public subscription.
The present proviso excludes a company which prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe for shares, but I do not believe that would afford the protection which is desired. A company may be a private company or a company not offering its bonds or shares for public subscriptions, although still not prohibiting such action. It might be, also, that the proposed provision is too broad, that any company could take advantage of the proviso by simply passing a resolution to the effect that public subscription is not to be invited. It seems to me if we confine the proviso to private companies or to other companies which, while not nominally private companies, do not in fact offer their stocks, shares or debentures to the public, that would be what this parliament would wish, and I move accordingly, seconded by the non. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling).

Mr. Chairman, I have
no particular desire to offer very harsh criticism of the proposal, but I do question the loosening up or the slackening of the present restrictions in connection with auditors participating in the management of * companies of which they are the auditors. I believe the principle is bad. If we are to do anything under the Companies Act or similar acts to affect auditing, we should make the position of the auditor clearer, more definite and more responsible than it is to-day. The value or merit of an auditor's report rests in the thoroughness with which his work is done. I have not the amendment in my hand, but from my memory of it I would draw attention to this possibility: a company might organize, publicly offer for sale its debentures and carry on business for a certain time with its auditors being permitted to act as directors. It might be the intention of the company to list its stock at some later date, which it could do by obtaining an amendment to its original charter. I desire only to draw attention to the danger of loosening the restrictions which already exist, which are meagre enough, as to auditors taking part in the management of companies of which they are auditors.

I have no desire to prolong the discussion on this bill, but I rise to say that I share fully the views expressed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). The Companies Act was amended at some length last year, and this is one of the matters which came before the committee. I believe there was unanimity in having our present act include a clause concerning this very matter. I think it appeals to everyone's common sense that a man who is an auditor of a company should not be a partner, associate or director of that company, otherwise he would be auditing his own accounts, and that is not a good principle. Subsection 3 of section 123 of the act reads as follows:
Neither the auditor of any company nor any partner associate in any accounting or auditing company or business with the said auditor shall be capable of being appointed a director or officer of the company.
That provision is as complete and extensive as it could be. It makes it very clear that the books of a company must be audited by someone who is not associated with or interested in the company. That is a good principle for all companies, and it should not be departed from even when dealing with private or small companies. They might as well not be audited as to be audited by one of their own personnel because, as I said before, if a man is a director of a company and is the auditor of that company, he is practically auditing his own work. I associate myself with the Minister of Trade and Commerce-and it is a great pleasure to associate with him-in opposing the amendment embodied in this section.

Mr. Chairman, it
seems to me that something very important is being lost sight of in the objections offered to this bill. Many companies which are practically family corporations are carrying on business throughout the country, and the purpose of any auditing they do is to audit the books of a servant of the company, such as the secretary treasurer. Instead of employing a firm of auditors or chartered accountants, these companies save money by auditing the books of their own officers. As the bill now stands, this practice would be made illegal. It seems to me that the present bill was meant to take care of situations such as this.

Mr. Chairman, there can be no doubt as to the wisdom of the enaet-ent of the last session. It is undesirable that the affairs of the company should be audited by those who are managing it, but it is not desired that legislation should react unfavourably against those whom it is intended to protect. When this subsection 3 was passed it was found that it wrought a great hardship on innumerable small com-
Companies Act-Auditors

panies. There is a large number of companies represented in Canada by auditors from the old land. They have offices here from which they transact business, but their affairs are controlled and supervised by auditors who are at the same time directors and managers of the companies. I am sure many hon. members can recall at least half a dozen such concerns in the larger cities of the Dominion. I venture to say that half of the hon. members in this house hold shares in small private companies, and this amendment is offered to enable those companies to carry on their business as they have in the past, without prejudicing the public, their neighbour or anyone else. It might be called a poor man's amendment; it offers that measure of elasticity which is desirable in all legislation if it is to be effective, and it need not reduce the quantum of supervision and careful scrutiny incidental to good business management. Large companies, companies in which public funds are invested and the shareholders of which must look to the auditors for protection, are in no way affected by this amendment. It applies only to private companies, and private companies are very insignificant entities as compared with those which the measure of last year aimed at protecting. If one were to take a census of the number of companies that are placed under a hardship by the legislation of last year, I think one would reach the conclusion that there is behind this amendment an element of wisdom and forbearance which makes it altogether desirable. It in no way attacks the principle to which the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) has referred.

The hon. gentleman referred
to a hardship. Is it the expense of outside auditors?

It is not only the expense of an outside audit. The people who own the company have to choose between being the auditors of the company, as stated, for instance, by the hon. member for East Algoma, for the purpose of auditing the accounts of their own business, and being ' directors of their own business. They are faced with that alternative.

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 1, the adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. Boulanger for the second, reading of Bill No. 18, to amend the Civil Service Act (returned soldiers' preference).

speakeroldname: Mr. W. W. KENNEDY (Winnipeg South Centre):
subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERANS RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I desire to make a few observations in connection with this bill which is sponsored by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger). It proposes to amend the Civil Service Act of Canada in two respects: first, by adding to section 29 of the said act a further subsection (5) reading as follows:
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this section, or in any regulations made by the Civil Service Commission, the preference mentioned in subsection 4 of this section shall be granted only in the case of Canadian nationals as defined in section 2 of chapter 21 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, or as defined in any amendment or reenactment thereof.
The explanatory note set out opposite this subsection in the bill reads:
The object of this subsection, which is new is to provide that the preference, commonly referred to as 'The returned soldiers' preference" shall be granted Canadian soldiers only.

Civil Service Act-Returned Soldiers
The second amendment proposed by the bill relates to section 33 of the act and has to do with the residence in Canada required as a condition precedent to the admission to examination of British subjects desirous of entering our civil service.
It is in respect to the first part of the bill that I wish to direct the immediate attention of the house. What is the purpose of the proposed amendment? I think I can do no better than give to the house the answer of the hon. member for Belle-chasse who is sponsoring the bill. As reported in Hansard at page 1196, the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) asked this question:
Is it the declared object of this bill to cut off the preference to veterans of the British army?
This is the reply of the hon. member for Bellechasse:
Yes. The intention is to restrict the preference to veterans of the Canadian army.
I ask the house to examine briefly that purpose, with some of its implications, in relation to the British Empire of which Canada is still, thank God, a part. This bill seeks .to draw a line of demarcation between Canadian nationals and all other soldiers of the empire who fought the battles of the empire in our hour of need. I know it is a far cry back to 1914, but I should like, if I could, to'take hon. members back for a few moments to those days so that they might realize in this year 1931 what was the situation in 1914 and by what means the empire met that crisis.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that it was not a prdblem for Canada alone, for the motherland alone, for Australia or New Zealand or South Africa alone, but it was an empire problem, and the keynote of the force with which that crisis was met was unity of force and purpose and not lines of demarcation. You will remember the call Chat went out in this country and how it was answered. From the little cabins of the miners along those creeks in the Yukon, from that great province of British Columbia, from the foothills of Alberta, from the plains of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, down through old Ontario to Quebec and the maritimes, who answered? Were they Canadian nationals alone? I ask hon. members to mark the calls that went out and to observe whether or not in those days the call was to Canadian nationals as distinct from imperials, and I shall give just a few of those slogans. What are they?
Hear the dead calling you, strong men and able
For Canada's honour respond to your name.
Here's your chance. It's men we want.
Each recruit brings peace nearer.
In her hour of need your country calls you.
Join the brave throng
That goes marching along.
Brothers, will you come?
The Prussians want to make this the dark continent. Will you let them do it?
"Fall in."
Answer now in your country's hour of need.
If ye break faith
We shall not sleep.
Boys, come over here. You are wanted.
You come across or Germany will.
Here is another one:
Young men!
The privilege of service is yours, that your country may live and that freedom may not disappear from the earth.
This one for the hon. member for Bellechasse :
Unis pour la paix avec la victoire.
Another:
It is always fair weather when good fellows get together. You will find a lot of good fellows in the Kilties. Why not join the 73rd Cameron Highlanders of Canada?
I want to place beside those slogans the words with which our troops were sped to the front. I want to give one extract from the speech of the late Sir Sam Hughes, then Minister of Militia, and a great minister he. was, to the troops at Gaspe, on October 2, 1914, as they were about to go:
That you will render a splendid account of yourselves for king and country is certain. You come of the right breed,-English, Scotch, Irish, French and Welsh.
No line of demarcation there. Again I should like to quote from the message of Sir Arthur Currie to the Canadian corps after the enemy had advertised its last great onslaught and had struck. You, Mr. Speaker, and many other hon. members of this house will keenly recall that message, which was dated March 27, 1918:
In an endeavour to reach an immediate decision the enemy has gathered all his forces and struck a mighty blow at the British army. Overwhelmed by sheer weight of numbers the British divisions in the line between the Scarpe and the Oise have fallen back fighting hard, steady and undismayed.
Measures have been taken successfully to meet this German onslaught. The French have gathered a powerful army, commanded by a most able and trusted leader and this army is now moving swiftly to our help. Fresh British divisions are being thrown in. The Canadians are soon to be engaged. Our motor machine gun brigade has already played a most gallant part and once again covered itself with glory.
Looking back with pride on the unbroken record of your glorious achievements, asking you to realize that to-day the fate of the British Empire hangs in the balance, I place my trust
1762	COMMONS
Civil Service Act-Returned Soldiers
in the Canadian corps, knowing that where Canadians are engaged there can be no giving way.
Under the orders of your devoted officers in the coming battle you will advance or fall where you stand facing the enemy.
Canadians, in this fateful hour, I command you and I trust you to fight as you have ever fought with all your strength, with all your determination, with all your tranquil courage. On many a hard fought field of battle you have overcome this enemy. With God's help you shall achieve victory once more.
A few days later all ranks were addressed by Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig, and I should like to put beside these extracts I have given his message to all ranks of the British army in France and Flanders. It is dated April 11, 1918:
Three weeks ago to-day the enemy began his terrific attacks against us on a fifty-mile front. His objects are to separate us from the French, to take the channel ports and destroy the British army.	. . .
In spite of throwing already 106 divisions into the battle and enduring the most reckless sacrifice of human life, he has as yet made little progress towards his goals.
We owe this to the determined fighting and self-sacrifice of our troops. Words fail me to express the admiration which I feel for the splendid resistance offered by all ranks of our army under the most trying circumstances.
Many amongst us now are tired. To those I would say that victory will belong to the side which holds out the longest. The French army is moving rapidly and in great force to our support.
There is no other course open to us but to fight it out. Every position must be held to the last man: there must be no retirement. With our backs to the wall and believing in the justice of our cause each one of us must fight on to the end. The safety of our homes and the freedom of mankind alike depend upon the conduct of each one of us at this critical moment.
In addition to those, Mr. Speaker, we have at the beginning of the story in the memorial tower in this building these words:
Read how free men throughout this land kept faith in the hour of trial and in the day of battle, remembering the traditions they had been taught, counting life nothing without liberty.
There answered the call' from this country 619,636 men. An analysis of those figures will prove of interest. Of those born in Canada there were 318,728; of those born in England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales and other British countries, 237,586; from other than British countries 59,505; not stated, 3,817. The call in those days was not to Canadian nationals alone, but to all citizens of the empire wherever dwelling. It is a matter of record that among the first to go from this country were many of those here from the motherland as well as many Canadians. From the farthest reaches of this country the British-born answer-

ed that call, and so anxious were they to rally to the mother country that many thousands of them at their own expense, paying their own transportation, left Canada to join their regiments in the old land.
This bill, if it passes this house, would now draw a line of demarcation between those who served in the Canadian army and the imperial veterans who served in the imperial army. I ask hon. gentlemen whether it is the desire of the people of Canada that this distinction should be drawn. I ask this house to remember that the preference given to all those who served in the allied armies, so far as the Civil Service Act as it now stands is concerned, was not prompted by charity but as a measure of re-establishment of those who served, and as such I submit that it should remain.
Last Sunday there took place in cemeteries in various cities and hamlets up and down this country the ceremony of burying exservice men who had died in various hospitals and elsewhere during the winter. The Last Post was sounded, the press was eulogistic of the services of these men, editorials were written.
I urge the hon. member for Bellechasse to reconsider this amendment. I would point out to him that already, with the lapse of time, even the youngest of those who served now border upon or have passed middle age. A few years more and with the flight of time all those who were united in those days of stress will again be united in death. Can Canada not wait a little longer?
The hon. member for Bellechasse appeals to this house in his closing words and purports to invoke the Canada first policy as enunciated by this government. Here is what he says:
I believe the spirit of the bill is in accordance with the Canada first policy of this government.
Let me remind him that the "devil can quote scripture for his purpose." The Canada First policy as enunciated by the Prime Minister of this country, and as I apprehend it. has to do with the welfare, happiness and prosperity of all Canada and of all who dwell therein, irrespective of origin, race, creed or party.
This amendment to the Civil Service Act proposes to draw a line between those who stood together and served our empire well in her great hour of need. I submit that the spirit of the bill is wrong. The bill is wrong and I protest against it: I trust that at the hands of this house it will receive "no quarter."

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERANS RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
All
of us, I think, appreciate the lofty and patriotic sentiments expressed by my hon. fr.end from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Kennedy). But
MA'/ 19, 1931
Civil Service Act

Returned Soldiers
the bill as submitted should at least be allowed to go to the committee in order to be carefully studied. If hon. members will turn to the provisions of the Civil Service Act, section 29, subsection 4, they will find that it deals with the preference given to returned soldiers, and I think they will agree with me that that section as it stands calls for some sort of amendment. I am not prepared to say that the amendment suggested by my hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) is the one which will meet the views of every member of this house, but I do think that if the bill is allowed to go to the committee, where proposals can be given careful consideration, amendments can be suggested which will meet with the approval of the majority of hon. members.
I will read the section of the Civil Service Act to which this bill refers. Section 29, subsection 4, reads:
In all examinations for entrance into the civil service the persons named on such special list who are found to possess the necessary-qualifications shall be named, in the order of merit, on the list of successful candidates above all other candidates; and all other persons who have been on active service overseas-
This is the list of persons preferred.
-on the military forces or who have served on the high seas in a seagoing ship of war in the naval forces of His Majesty, or of any of the allies of His Majesty, during the war, who have left such service with an honourable record or who have been honourably discharged, or when any persons who have served as aforesaid have died owing to such service, the widows of such persons, and who, in either case, obtain sufficient marks to pass such examinations, shall, irrespective of the marks they have obtained, be named in the order of merit, on the list of successful candidates next after any candidates who are on the special list mentioned in subsection two of this section and above all other candidates.
The act as very badly drafted. I do not know who drafted it, but with all respect I must say a terrible mess has been made of its English. In any case it means that on the preferred list, apparently indiscriminately, there shall be placed all those who served in the forces of His Majesty, naval or military, as well as all those who served in the forces of armies allied to His Majesty's.
I believe a number of the members of this house will agree with me that, whatever patriotic motives we may have had at that time in inserting such a provision, it is no longer necessary that we should give a preference to those who served in the allied forces. Let me give an example which, while it may be personal, I believe will apply to other members of this house who served overseas. I have a son of seventeen. In
another year or two he will be eligible to enter the Civil Service of Canada. I hope and pray he will never desire to do so, but the fact is that he will in due course become eligible. Should he desire to enter the civil service he will be obliged to submit to a preference in favour of a Portuguese or a French Senegalese or some other soldier who at some time or other served in the allied forces. This seems to me absolutely ridiculous. There is no reason why the children of Canadian returned soldiers should be obliged to give precedence to some one who served in any one of the allied forces.

speechtext:
Such men may come to Canada and, provided they have the residential qualifications, having become British subjects perhaps only two or three years ago, just long enough to make them Canadian nationals, may have the preference over children of returned Canadian soldiers. I submit that the act as originally drawn, in section 29, subsection 4, should be changed; and if this bill is allowed to go into committee I propose to submit an amendment which will eliminate the preference given to members of the allied forces. So far as members of the imperial forces are concerned, I would propose this amendment:
In all examinations for entrance into the civil service, the persons named on such special list, who are found to possess the necessary qualifications, shall be named in the order of merit on the list of successful candidates above all other candidates, and all other persons who have been on active service overseas, in the military or naval forces of His Majesty during the late war, and were at the time of their enlistment-
This covers the 30,000 mentioned by my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre.
-oi at the date of passing of this act-
That is, the present time.
-domiciled in Canada, who have left such service with an honourable record, or who have been honourably discharged, or when any persons who have served overseas as aforesaid, have died owing to such service, the widows of such persons, and who, in either case, obtained sufficient marks to pass such examinations, shall, irrespective of the marks they

Beauharnois-Miss Macphail
have obtained, be named in the list of successful candidates next after any candidates who are in the special list mentioned in subsection 2 of this section, and above all other candidates.
The proposal is first of all to eliminate the preference given to members of the allied forces and, secondly, to give a preference to members of the imperial forces who were domiciled in Canada at the time, of enlistment or who are at the present time-at the date of the passing of this act-domiciled in the Dominion. That is to say, it is not intended to give a preference to those who may come here after the passing of the act.
That is the proposal which I hope to make if the bill goes to committee. It is a proposal which I believe will commend itself to many members of this house who may be under the impression that the bill now under consideration is designed to do away with the returned soldier preference. I believe an amendment such as I have suggested would fully safeguard all those returned soldiers whom it is the interest of this house to protect.
