subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Gardiner.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey): I shall address the house very briefly, and I wish to do so because, in my opinion, it has been too often true that the natural resources of Canada have been given away to promoters. This policy, which we have followed fairly consistently in the past, has created millionaires on the one hand and struggling Canadian citizens on the other; and it is because I believe that the Beauharnois project comes within this classification that I wish to discuss it. There seems to be something in the nature of giving away the natural resources of Canada.
In the first place, as has been made clear in this house many times, both in this debate and in former discussions, the prospectus made claims that could not be substantiated by the racts. It does seem clear that the Beauharnois corporation could not have sold their bonds as successfully as they did, or possibly could not have sold them at all, had it not been that the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario entered into a long-term contract with

them to take 250,000 horse-power. It is curious to find that the hydro-electric enterprise, the pride of all those who stand for public ownership in Canada, should have put itself in this position. We recall that Sir Adam Beck when he founded the enterprise wanted, through it, to develop the water powers of the province for the use of the people at cost. Those of us who were in the house when Mr. Church was a member knew what an avowed friend of public ownership he always was. In an interview as reported in the Toronto Globe of Tuesday, April 14, 1931, I find he said in relation to the hydro-electric commission:
It could not have been put over-
That is, the Beauharnois project.

without Mr. Ferguson's guarantee to take
250.000	horse-power, which guarantee financed the whole deal.
In following other utterances on this subject, one can hardly miss the interview that Mr. Sinclair, the Liberal leader in Ontario, or the former Liberal leader-I am not quite clear on this point-gave to the Toronto Globe, as reported in its issue of April 22, 1931. He said :
Hydro agreed to purchase 250,000 horsepower from Beauharnois, another block of
150.000	horse-power was contracted for by another concern. These contracts enabled Beauharnois bonds to be sold. Their prospectus showed these contracts would pay more than all operating expenses and the interest and sinking fund on all the bond issues. There remains 100,000 horse-power still to be marketed at a clear profit. Such being the case, hydro is buying power at more than its cost of production, and the excess over cost goes to the promoters of Beauharnois.
And may I add for Mr. Sinclair-at the expense of the people of Ontario. Then, too, Mr. McQuibban, speaking in the Ontario legislature, used this very significant sentence as reported in the Toronto Globe of March 30 last:
Hydro has hoisted the white flag of surrender.
It really does look like that. A public ownership scheme started, as I said a moment ago, to develop power at cost, has become a distributing corporation for private concerns -concerns that have no particular interest in developing power at cost, but rather in developing power at profit. So I believe I can say without fear of contradiction that the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario has aided and abetted the schemes of its adversaries. If more power is needed in Ontario why is it not possible to develop the power resources of the international section of the St. Lawrence river? That would seem

to me to be a policy in keeping with the practice of the hydro-electric commission in years gone by.
There is one other aspect of the question with respect to which I wish to say a word or two. The development of the Beauharnois project, in the opinion of those who have given most study to it, prevents the development of the St. Lawrence waterway. It naturally occurs to one that if a depth , of 35 feet is needed for ocean boats below Montreal, the same depth would be needed above Montreal. May I again refer to Mr. Church? And one must say this for him. that as we look back over his record in the house we cannot help but feel that . many times he championed causes here when they were very unpopular, and that he did it because he believed it to be in the best interests of his own city and province that he loves so much and of the whole Dominion. In this connection he said, as reported in the Toronto Globe of April 14, 1931:
There will be no St. Lawrence waterway. The whole public canal policy of Canada has been upset by this deal and the company given power to build an artificial navigation canal 27 feet deep on the St. Lawrence in exchange for the power, whereas from Montreal to Quebec the navigation channel is 35 feet. The canal feature is a myth.
Then Mr. Sinclair in the same interview to which I have already referred stated:
In the Beauharnois development, the depth oi the ship canal is limited to 27 feet. Below Montreal the river is now being dredged to a depth of 35 feet to allow large ocean boats to reach .Montreal, which will thus become the head of navigation for all such vessels. If it is good for Montreal, would it not be good for all ports in Ontario, including the 840,000,000 harbour of Toronto? The construction of the ship canal also provides for fixed spans in bridges crossing^ it, indicating there is no thought of navigation using the canal, because all other canals will remain as at present, and can be used as at present for all traffic west of Montreal. Montreal seems to control the situation, and promoters of Beauharnois have seen to it that navigation in a big way stops at Montreal.
And Mr. McQuibban speaking in the legislature of Ontario, as reported in the Toronto Globe of March 20, 1931, said:
If this gigantic scheme-
Speaking of the Beauharnois scheme.
-is consummated it has postponed the seaway for one, or maybe more, generations.
It seems clear that the fact of the Ontario Hydro-Electric Power commission buying power from Quebec for a period of fifteen years will in itself retard the development, of the deep waterway. For that period of time at least Ontario will not be in a position
Beauharnois-Mr. Campbell
to buy power from the international section of the St. Lawrence should it be developed-Then, too, Quebec can claim that since she is exporting this great block of power to the province of Ontario she is short of power for her own use, and so can bring pressure to bear upon the Dominion government to allow her the full flow of the river.
I would not have said a word as the Prime Minister has agreed to a parliamentary committee to investigate the whole Beauharnois scheme, except that I do feel tha-t since the inception of the hydro-electric enterprise in Ontario the danger to its continuance as a public-owned enterprise has never been as grave as it is at the moment, and I believe that all lovers of public ownership in Ontario should bring to bear whatever influence they have as a whole to ensure that if possible the contract is cancelled, and certainly that the present policy of the hydro-electric commission shall not be followed in the future.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to discuss at any great length the history of the Beauharnois project. That has been very well covered by hon. members in this corner of house who have preceded me. Suffice it to say that the development of power on the St. Lawrence river has been conceded to the province of Quebec with regard to that part of the river lying in that province. Under the constitution, however, the federal government controls navigable rivers. I know there are some legal arguments in connection with these, points, but in substance that is the attitude which has been taken by the federal government in regard to this question. Therefore the power rights that were granted to the Beauharnois company by the province of Quebec were of no use to that company until they secured the authority of the federal government to use the water of the river. The federal government granted the right to the company to divert 40,000 cubic feet per second from the St. Lawrence river -to their fifteen-mile power canal. This will enable the company to develop 500,000 horse-power of electrical energy, with an annual commercial value of about S15 per horse-Dower.
The government secured nothing in return for the granting of this natural resource, and the late King government has been very severely criticised for its failure to secure some compensation. However, the company are obligated to permit navigation through that canal if required. That navigation, however, will be made possible only by the construction of locks, which it is estimated will cost about $25,000,000. Perhaps the most severe criticism

Beauharnoi<?*-Mr. Campbell
of the action of the late government is that they did not stipulate for the construction of these locks by the company. This criticism is accentuated by the fear that this diversion may interfere with the development of the St. Lawrence deep waterways scheme. Since the United States has treaty rights in the St. Lawrence river, also, it is even asserted in some quarters that there may be international complications.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in connection with the deep waterways development there, would seem to be three courses open to us in regard to the navigation of this river. First there is the present Soulanges canal, about fifteen miles long, on the north shore of the river, which will accommodate vessels drawing fourteen feet of water. All the navigation of that portion of the river going around the rapids must use that canal at present. The Beau-harnois power canal when completed, will accommodate vessels drawing twenty-seven feet of water, and this canal also is about fifteen miles in length. This may or may not conform to the requirements of the engineers of the deep waterways scheme. If it does, then I presume the canal can be used, but I am not quite clear on that point. I have heard it asserted that it does conform to the requirements of the scheme, and on the other hand I have heard it said that it does not. There is also a shorter canal suggested by the joint board of engineers, which would be about five miles in length, and at the head of which there could be developed about 2,000,000 horsenpower.
It seems to me that in dealing with this question parliament first must see that nothing is done which may interfere with navigation on the river. I think that is the first thing that must be decided, and that should be consistent with the development of the maximum amount of electrical energy. Electrical energy is one of Canada's most valuable assets; it is one of the things which we expect to give Canada her place in the industrial world in the years to come, and I believe I am safe in saying that no other country in the world is possessed of the great potential water power which we have in Canada. Therefore II say that in any scheme of this kind we must first protect navigation and in the second place we must consider the development of the maximum amount of electrical power.
The obvious duty of parliament, therefore, is to secure something for the people for the valuable rights which have been granted to the company. So far in the debate only one suggestion has been put forward, namely that the whole undertaking be cancelled, on the assumption that the government itself would

operate the development. That could be done, if the government has a legal right, as has been asserted, by the cancellation of the present rights granted to the company; or it could be done by the government declaring the whole work to be for the general good of Canada. In either case I assume the. government would be called upon to reimburse some of those who have put their money into this project, at least those to whom the Prime Minister referred as the innocent third parties.
It seems to me, however, that there is an alternative. The history of governmental action in Canada in the past would give us very little hope that any such cancellation will be. made. The alternative, it would seem to me, would be to grant the extra diversion requested on condition of a consideration therefor, possibly the construction of some public work which would adequately and properly protect the public interest and give the people of Canada something in exchange for the valuable concession made.
With regard to the question of cancelling the project, as the Prime Minister has indicated there would be difficulties. There is the question of financing; there are the innocent third parties, the persons to whom bonds have been sold and by whom common stock has been purchased. Then again there is the question of operation. If the government took it over it would have to build up an organization to operate it. Whether or not we have enough confidence in ourselves and in the government to undertake a great work of this kind is a matter open to question. Then there is another point in regard to the lease of power. I understand the company has already contracted for all the power it proposes to develop. Industries are being built up and developed on the strength of these contracts, so the ramifications of the enterprise are very great and the whole thing is very complicated.
Now lei us consider the second proposition, that we should secure something from the company in return for what has been granted to them. In that connection it seems to me the difficulties are not so great. The question is simply what we can secure for the people as adequate compensation for the right that has been granted the company. Let me. say again that any [DOT] arrangement entered into must make absolutely certain that navigation is not prejudicially affected. The Soulanges canal, I think it is admitted, is not suitable for the deep waterways scheme; that canal would have to be reconstructed or entirely rebuilt in order to fit in with that proposition. Probably the Beauharnois canal comes much closer to the specifications any such canal

Beauharnois-Mr. Campbell
would be required to meet. In this connection I would like, to draw the attention of hon. members of the house to two very excellent articles appearing in the Manitoba Free Press, and written by a man named It. K. Finlyason. These articles show a very thorough and thoughtful study of the whole question, both from the standpoint of navigation and with regard to the development of power, and I would commend them to hon. members. The first article appeared in the Manitoba Free Press under date of December 19, 1930, and deals more particularly with the question of navigation. Referring to power, however, Mr. Finlayson says:
Harnessing power presents the same economic difficulty that would follow if an equal number of horses *walked out of the stream. They must be used, or destroyed, or sold abroad. It will require some 30 to 40 years in Canada to absorb the St. Lawrence Canadian power into use.
There is another problem also. The company securing the right to develop power must secure a market for that power, because there is no use developing power unless it can be sold.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: The Prime Minister having promised an investigation into this matter, what is the object of all this discussion which is taking place now?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will just listen until I am through I will tell him the object. I think we have a right to discuss the question here, and to perhaps give some lead to the committee.
Dealing with freight rates, Mr. Finlayson says:
The picture of all the great vessels of the world coming to Port Arthur has vanished, and with it those fanciful claims for savings which were to equal the present cost of shipment from Port Arthur to Montreal.
His argument is that from a navigation standpoint the project is not feasible; it is feasible only by the development of power supplementary to navigation. Dealing with transportation, he says:
But while transportation is arguing, power considerations are acting.
He then goes on to give the details of the grants to the Beauharnois company. Referring to the rights to divert water granted to the company, he says:
If the main river development for navigation is feasible in spite of this diversion and is eventually followed, the Dominion of Canada without any consideration whatsoever has surrendered such right to revenue as it had from P00.000 hydro electric power with a preemption of the power market in the St. Lawrence basin for five years.
Editorials appeared in the Manitoba Free Press apparently inspired by and based upon the articles from which I have just quoted. An editorial in the Free Press of December 20, 1930, in part reads as follows:
The present condition of the waterways question is well described in the articles contributed to the Free Press by Mr. R. K. Finlayson. The surrender by the King government of the Dominion position-outlined by Mr. Lapointe in his statement of 1927-in the face of political pressure from Ontario and Quebec, the absence of any political support from other parts of Canada, and the failure of the supreme court to give a clear judgment upon the questions submitted to it, as indicated by its action in the matter of the Beauharnois lease, has placed the whole enterprise in jeopardy, as is clearly shown by Mr. Finlayson. The advantages of the canal are not sufficient to justify the people of Canada in building it out of the public funds, without assistance from water-power rentals. Whether the Dominion's right to share in the power which it creates can be regained is doubtful.
Another editorial which appeared in the issue of April 29, 1931, in part reads as follows :
The whole Beauharnois situation is to be reviewed in Ottawa this session, and there is still time to snatch safety for the seaway from the elutches of the hitherto invincible power interests.
There has been too much politics in the Beauharnois situation up to the present. The primary aim is too often lost sight of. The St. Lawrence deep waterway project must be carried to completion. This is the aspect of the situation which is national in character. The disposition of St. Lawrence power, save as it affects the seaway, is not a national nroblem. It happens, however, to be the only lever with which the seaway can be built.
That is the particular point to the whole argument. The editorial continues:
The power on the Canadian section of the St. Lawrence is in the right of the Quebec government, which can dispose of it as it sees fit.
And again:
The Dominion has the right to step into the situation and say that not another horsepower shall be installed at Beauharnois until plans are adequately laid, and under way, for the development of the whole St. Lawrence scheme. If Mr. Bennett does not do this, lie will betray his election pledges.
And further on the editorial continues:
He has the chance to block further grants to Beauharnois until such time as the whole seaway is assured.
If he does not care to take so drastic a step, another course lies open to Mr. Bennett. He can drive a bargain with the Beauharnois interests such as should have been driven by the King government. He can say to them that they can take more water, but only if they hand over not only a fully equipped canal on the Beauharnois section, but also the necessary
1768	COMMONS
Beauharnois-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)
canals ancl locks on the Lachine section further down the river. He can force the Beauharnois interests to do this, or refuse to make them any further grants.
It seems to me that that is the real crux of the whole situation. I agree with the suggestion made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) that this matter should be sent to a committee of the house for further investigation. Hon. members should be allowed to interview these men in order to ask questions. They should come here, place their cards on the table and give us all the information we need to discuss this matter intelligently. We would not have been in possession of all the information we now have in connection with the Beauharnois project had it not been for a rival financial group who had been worsted in the fight for this power. Both these financial groups should be called before the committee and asked to give us all the information they possess. It should be discovered whether or not the present Beauharnois canal will adequately serve the needs of navigation for the purposes of the St. Larvrence deep waterway. Technical advice should be available as to what should be secured to the people of Canada in exchange for the company being allowed to go ahead.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming as I do from the city of Montreal only twenty-five miles from the Beauharnois canal, and in view of the fact that a great many distinguished citizens of that city are directly or indirectly concerned with the Beauharnois project and are working for its completion, I rise not to protest against the motion of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) that an investigation be made of this project, but to say that I believe such an investigation will be welcomed as much by those connected with the Beauharnois Company as by those making the charges.
Hon. members should realize that this is one of the biggest projects ever undertaken by Canadians. Next to the Panama canal, it is possibly the biggest canal in the world. It will cost in the neighbourhood of some $75,000,000 when completed. I do not protest against the charges made this afternoon by the hon. member for Acadia, but in making those charges he must realize that the responsibility rests upon him and other hon. members in his corner of the house.
Several questions will be involved in any investigation regarding Beauharnois. In dealing with this subject the hon. member for Acadia referred to a citizen of Montreal, an outstanding engineer, a man with a genius for engineering possessed by very few Canadians, and who has worked eighteen years on this

project. That man is attacked in the. House of Commons by the hon. member for Acadia in these words: Sweezey and his associates are trying to acquire certain rights by fraud and conspiracjr. The hon. member must realize the full purport of those words. When the investigation, suggested by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is being conducted, I hope the hon. member will then make his charges as they should be made, directly to the people charged. They should be given an opportunity to defend themselves against the charges, the evidence of which the hon. member claims to possess. Unless the charges are made in such manner, the purpose of asking hon. members to acquiesce in his demands is useless, the fact being that he along with other members in that comer of the house had ample time during the last two years to make those charges. I have no doubt that the action of hon. members in that comer of the house is in their view to all intents and purposes fully justified. I have full faith in their integrity, but I might say that the house is entitled to be given in no uncertain terms the facts upon which those charges have been based. First of all, the charges against those associated with the Beauharnois proposition should be clearly set forth, because charges have been made against them. Charges have been made against members of the upper house, the Senate, and those charges should be set forth in no uncertain terms. Charges have been made against hon. members on the opposition side, and possibly against hon. members on this side of the house, and those charges should be fully explained. Charges have also been made against the judiciary. Occasion was taken to refer to some lawsuits that are pending in the courts of Quebec, and I trust the hon. member for Acadia will be just as frank in making those charges against the judiciary of that province.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I did not make any
charge against the judiciary of Quebec. I merely made a statement with regard to press reports.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Acadia, if my memory serves me aright, mentioned the name of Acting Chief Justice Greenshields of the province of Quebec, and he must have had some reason for mentioning that gentleman's name. Will he, in making his charges, explain if he made any charges against the acting chief justice or will he make it quite clear why the acting chief justice's name was mentioned?
I do not intend to dwell upon the vastness of the Beauharnois project. As I stated, it

Beauharnois-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)
is the greatest undertaking ever contemplated by Canadians. I was thoroughly amazed by what the undertaking really meant. There is in operation at the Beauharnois plant one piece of machinery costing more than half a million dollars, and there has been expended on machinery alone more than $5,500,000 so far. For excavation purposes material has been removed amounting to more than 4,000,000 cubic yards. During the past year-and this is a very important matter for the city of Montreal-2,200 men have been on the payrolls every month, and at present 3,000 men are employed with an estimate of 3,000 other men making materials for the Beauharnois project. I am bringing these facts to the hon. member's attention, so that he may realize that, in submitting this question to the house he is making a very serious charge and one which affects Canadians everywhere. It affects not only the rights of Quebec but also the rights of the Dominion, and it is a question which, if it is possible for an investigation to settle it, should be settled by such a method. If the people connected with the project are not given a fair chance to proceed with their work, the work will be stopped and some action should then be taken whereby their interests and those of the people who have invested money in the Beauharnois project will be protected. I think hon. members in that corner of the house are assuming a little too much in advance that this canal will be taken over by the government. We in the province of Quebec, rightly or wrongly, have so far believed in private ownership. We may, be wrong. The people of Ontario may believe in public ownership, but strange as it may seem, the Beauharnois promoters, out of the 500,000 horse-power which they propose to develop, have already sold to Ontario by contract 250,000 horse-power.
Mr. LaVERGNE :	Does my hon. friend
contend that we in Quebec believe the navigation of the St. Lawrence should be in the hands of a private company?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I do not intend to enter into any argument with my hon. friend regarding the navigation question, but my hon. friend surely realizes that the canal, which, when completed, will be twenty-seven feet deep, should take care of any navigation to the sea.
Mr. LaVERGNE: Undoubtedly.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
The channel from Montreal to Quebec, as my hon. friend knows, is not as deep as that.
Mr. LaVERGNE: Undoubtedly; but will it be the property of a private company and not of the Dominion.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Surely my hon. friend realizes that neither the Beauharnois company nor any other private company will control navigation so far as Canada is concerned. No government would be so foolish as to permit navigation of the St. Lawrence to be left in the hands of any private corporation. There would be something wrong with any government that would handle that particular problem in such a way.
I come to a more serious part of this question, and I hesitate to make the statement. I am not interested in the Beauharnois; I am not retained iby the Beauharnois, nor have I any connection with the Beauharnois. I am interested in Montreal, and I am interested in the development of Beauharnois if it is going to bring industries into the vicinity of Montreal. When that company has expended more than $5,000,000 in industrial lands, proposing to bring industries to Montreal and to give them power cheaper than it can be had in any other country on the face of the earth, naturally I should like to see such a project proceed to completion. That is the primary abject which those of us have who look to the future of the Beauharnois development I know nothing about the financing of it.
I am going to enlighten my hon. friend in regard to the other side of the picture. He has put forward certain views; undoubtedly he believes that they have been presented to him by people who have given him the facts. The facts of Beauharnois as I understand them are these: The original rights, as mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), were in the hands of one Robert. Robert had a charter from the Quebec government as far back as 1910. That was the Beauharnois Light, Heat <?: Power Company. Robert gave an option to the Transportation and Power Company for $10,000. Now comes the controversial question: Did he give an option or did he sell the rights to the land? On one side you have certain clients claiming he gave an option, and on the other the Transportation and Power Company claiming they bought the land. Naturally the hon. member for Acadia and those on the left will agree that the only way that question could be settled was in the courts. They went to the courts and after a decision had been given in Robert's favour, Mr. Sweezey and those associated with him, I understand, proceeded to deal with Robert Was that the end of the matter? Not at all. From then on the people who were dealing with Robert in the first instance immediately began their attacks on Sweezey and Beauharnois. Mr. Sweezey and those associated
1770	COMMONS
Beauharnois-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)
with him went to the Quebec government for an extension of their charter rights. That involves another question that will have to be decided as between the provincial and federal governments. He got the powers under his charter extended for the widening of the canal and for the diversion of more water from lake St. Francis to lake St. Louis, as well as the right to build a power house on lake St. Louis instead of on the river St. Louis He proceeded with that work.
The financing of this company was not done in a day. Four months after the actual construction work was started the first public financing was done. Several months later my hon. friend from Acadia brought this matter up in the house. I do not want to reflect in any way upon the intergrity of hon. members in that corner of the house. I wish to make that quite plain, but it does seem strange to me that all the time that Sweezey and those connected with the Beauharnois project were engaged in this gigantic engineering scheme, the greatest ever launched in Canada, involving the diversion of the railway line of the New York Central, the building of a bridge-

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Two bridges.
Mr. BEiLL (St. Antoine): -the making of arrangements with four different townships so that the public roadway could pass, they should at the same time be faced with attacks from these other men who claimed that they had no rights to the canal proposition at all. An action was taken in the courts against those associated with the Beauharnois company to the amount of $7,000,000. What happened to that action? It was tried by Mr. Justice Duclos, and as my hon. friend from Acadia knows, on the second day of the trial the plantiffs desisted from the action. The principals of the Beauharnois company must have then felt that they were through with these constant attacks which were being made upon them. But a few months later an action was brought against the company or its associates in the amount of $10,000,000. It is not fair for the members sitting in that corner of the house to get up and accuse all those interested in Beauharnois. I am not at all concerned in the political faith of any member so far as this particular project is concerned. But there is another side to this picture. These men who have been bringing these actions at law have access to the courts. I refer particularly to Cantin, Regan, the Transportation and Power Company, and to Ecremont, none of whom is known to me, but these men claim, and my information comes

from as reliable a source as I believe is open to hon. gentlemen in that corner of the house, that amounts running from one million down were demanded for settlement; otherwise they would bring the matter u>p on the floor of the House of Commons.
The hon. member for Acadia has made his charges on the floor of the House of Commons, and has been promised a committee for the investigation of the charges against the Beauharnois company. I want him to be fair towards those associated with that project and to put everything before the committee in the most straightforward manner. I feel sure that he will do so. There is no reason so far as I can see why this investigation should not settle once and for all the question of provincial and federal rights so far as Beauharnois is concerned, and why the people who have invested their money in Beauharnois should not be given a fair opportunity to see the project develop. As I say it is a project owned by Canadians, financed by Canadians, in Canadian territory, and built for the purpose of attracting industries and providing them with the cheapest power in the world. I do not see why thousands of men should be thrown out of employment, and their families made to suffer for a day longer than is absolutely necessary, and I appeal to the right hon. the Prime Minister, as soon as the charges have been properly brought forward, to expedite this investigation and let us have an end of it, and the settling once for all of this Beauharnois argument about which we have heard so much

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
It is not my intention to dwell at great length on the arguments which have been adduced by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner), the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) and' other hon. members who have spoken in this debate, but there are one or two phases of the argument to which I should like for a short time to direct the attention of the house.
First of all may I invite attention to the argument made by the hon. member for Bow River, an argument following somewhat the line of his remarks on the subject a year ago except that his main argument to-day is that there was no right in the federal government to approve of plans for the diversion of water. The hon. member made a speech in his usual excellent manner on this very subject during the session of 1930, but then he never raised the main argument which he has used to-day as one of his objections to the scheme. Today it is his main objection, that the government had no jurisdiction to approve of the

Beauharnois-Mr. Elliott
plans, that the Minister of Public Works and the government in granting approval were going beyond their jurisdiction. He cited section 4 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act in proof of his statement. May I read section 4 of that act, which has been read already a couple of times:
No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site thereof has been approved by the governor in council, nor unless such work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council.
That is what he based his whole argument upon. Apparently he has not read paragraph (b) of section 2 of the act, which defines "work" as follows:
.... "work" includes any bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, wharf, dock, pier or other structure, tunnel or pipe, or telegraph or power cable or wive and the approaches or other works necessary or appurtenant thereto, or any work, structure or device, whether similar in character to the foregoing or not, which may interfere with navigation.
If my recollection serves me aright, that last part was inserted after the act had been in force a couple of years so as to make it cover practically everything. That act has been administered ever since by a department of this government; diversions of water have been granted under its term's and have been dealt with by the various governments which have been in power in this country since that time. That I want to make perfectly clear. There is, I submit, no work that might interfere with navigation which is not covered under this act; and I think it will appeal to hon. members of this house that the spirit of the act could not be carried out if any . work which might possibly interfere with navigation were omitted from the purview of that legislation.
What was the position of the government when this application was made? My hon. friend from Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) spoke about the policy of public ownership. That matter, I may say, had been settled when the application was made. This was water belonging to the province of Quebec Unless it belongs to the province of Quebec, then there is no approval granted for diversion of it. The terms of the order in council make that perfectly clear. I do not wish to deal in detail with the terms of the order in council, but all reasonable safeguards which could have been taken will be found upon investigation to have been taken. The lease which was brought to the government by the applicant was a lease from the province of Quebec of such flow of the river St. Lawrence
at that particular point, not exceeding 40,000 cubic feet per second, as belonged to the province. It was not water that belonged to the Dominion of Canada; it was not water over which the Dominion had jurisdiction, except in so far as navigation was concerned.
That application was brought in, and the whole question for the department to decide was as to whether or not that 40,000 cubic feet of water per second could be diverted without interfering with navigation. That was an engineering problem which it took months to settle definitely; and the duty of the department, and of the government of which that department was a part, was to refuse to approve of the plans if it was going to interfere with navigation. And the duty was just as obvious to approve of the plans if it did not interfere with navigation.
The matter was reported upon by the most competent engineers in the land-and I believe my hon. friend the present Minister of Public Works will agree with me that they are very competent engineers in that department. They were very busy and they called in the assistance of other engineers, most capable men; and after very careful consideration they decided that if certain safeguards were observed they would approve of these plans, provided the water were diverted by a channel. And the channel is defined, I think, as 600 feet in width. It will be one of the best canals in the world, a canal which will not only not interfere with navigation but which will make for better navigation than there is at the present time along any other section of the St. Lawrence anywhere in that district.
So that so far as navigation is concerned, those interested are. amply protected by the conditions which were imposed at the time the plans were approved. So far as the province of Quebec is concerned, they have rights to whatever water belongs to them and over which they have control. And they have a right to have the government say whether or not the plan that they propose shall be followed. What would be the position of this government if a lessee should come to them and say, "I have a lease from the province of Quebec of certain water rights. If the rights do not belong to the province they are not covered by this lease, but we want approval by you of plans to divert such waters as are owned by the province of Quebec". Suppose they put forth plans which our engineers inform us are sufficient to provide for these waters and to give good navigation -and I do not think anyone will contend that it will not be the very best navigation possible; the government, I sumbit, has no alter*
Beauhamois-~Mr. Elliott

speechtext:
My hon. friend has great
faith. I think he is right. But there is a certain bank of land left at the point from which the water is to be diverted, and that, I understand, will not be taken away until the plans are all thoroughly approved by the minister. I do not understand that any of the water has been diverted up to the present time.
I had not intended to speak at any length, and I' am very glad that the Prime Minister has intimated that he will have the matter referred to a committee. I hope that, in looking into the question, the committee will go thoroughly into every aspect of it which has been brought up from time to time by various critics of this scheme.
I wish to say just one word more. When the debate took place a year ago on the motion of the hon. member for Acadia to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of urgency, the motion was withdrawn. The matter was one of urgent importance at that time and

apparently, a year later, it is still urgent, only, the urgency is of a little different nature from what it was at that particular time. Several of the reasons for the urgency were not given at that time.
I think it is well in business matters-and this is one of the most important that ever came before any department of government- that they should be thoroughly considered, and I am confident that when the committee go carefully into the matter they will be satisfied that the most complete safeguards were placed around the approval of the plans and the manner in which the water was to be diverted.
There is some question, of course, as to the ownership of the whole flow of the St. Lawrence, which, if I recollect correctly, is about 200,000 cubic feet per second. Part of this flow had been leased to various . other concerns, and' with the 40,000 cubic feet per second leased to the Beauharnois company there still remains a balance perhaps double what this diversion amounts to. But the government could not justify waiting to have the question of ownership settled, for the reason that when the matter was before the supreme court hon. members will recall that their lordships stated in effect: "We cannot find specifically upon the points submitted to us. We must have a concrete case. We are not going to give judgment upon theories. When a concrete case arises it will be decided, and until then it cannot be decided." So that the absolute ownership of all the flow of water cannot be settled until a concrete case arises and is decided by the courts. But this portion of the river being situated entirely in the province of Quebec, I think there can be no question that at least the 40,000 cubic feet proposed to be diverted by this particular work will prove to be the property of that province. If mot, we are protected by the order in council, and the right to divert ceases upon any judgment being given by the supreme court that the whole or any portion of the water does not belong to the province of Quebec.
I do not propose to discuss the matter further at the present time. I have no doubt it will be thrashed out before the committee. But I did want to place before the house in as fair a way as I could just what question was submitted to the department and just what position the department took in dealing with it. The action taken was in accordance with what has been the practice of the depart-

Beauharnou-Mr. Euler
ment for years, and I think the committee will find that the department acted with as much care at least as has been exercised in any similar case which has ever come before it.
Mr. LaVERGNE : Will my hon. friend allow me a question on the ownership of the water? Suppose the department had come to the conclusion that the water to be diverted belonged to the Dominion, would the late government have granted the permit to the Beauhamois company?

speechtext:
Of course my hon. friend is asking me the same kind of question that the supreme court refused to answer, and I think I should follow the precedent then established.
Mr. LaVERGNE : Their case was not yours.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure that I can add anything of value to the discussion which has taken place, but apart entirely from the interest which a member should take in a question of some importance, I have perhaps a peculiar interest from various points of view. In the first place, I happen to come from the province of Ontario, which perhaps more than any other, with the exception of the province of Quebec, is interested in the development and use of this power from the St. Lawrence river. In the second place, I am and have always been a strong advocate of public ownership-public ownership of water powers, natural resources and other services which are in a sense monopolistic, or may become monopolistic, and upon which the prosperity and welfare of the people generally depend. I have always felt that in such cases I would even go further than we have gone in this country in some respects. I have always felt that water powers and other services of like nature should remain, if not in the ownership and operation of the people themselves, at least very definitely under the control of the people. Then, finally, I have a peculiar interest in the question because I happened to be a member of the government which passed the order in council that we are now considering.
As I have said, I have always been predisposed to public ownership, and when the matter of the Beauharnois lease came up I, for one, as did most of my colleagues in the government of that day, hesitated to pass the order in council, not feeling quite sure whether we had the right to do so, and it was only when I felt satisfied that we had not only the power but were under a moral 22110-113
obligation to issue the order in council, that as a member of the government I consented to the passing of the order.
The matter then to my mind had to be considered from three points of view: first of all, that the water power does belong to the provinces; second, that the 42,000 cubic feet per second allotted did not interfere with the navigation of the river; third, that the government had legal authoritiy to pass the order in council. I am not a lawyer, I am not an engineer, and so far as I was concerned I felt, as also I think did most of my colleagues in the government of the day. that we had to take the advice and the opinion of those who were best qualified to judge in these technical matters.
Mention has been made of the 'reference to the supreme court of questions in regard to the ownership of these water powers as between the provinces and the Dominion. While no definite opinion was given by the supreme court, I think it was pretty well understood from the judicial deliverance later handed down that water powers situated entirely within a province do belong to the province itself. I do submit that with respect to a stream which is not navigable and is entirely within the borders of a province the water power does undoubtedly belong to the province; therefore it is logical to conclude that where a navigable stream is entirely within the confines of a province, the water power should also belong to the province so long as navigation is conserved.
I might say further-and perhaps in this my right hon. leader will correct me-that I think we, as a government, also came to the conclusion that as a matter of policy and as a matter of moral right it was advisable and proper that the water-powers of any stream, whether navigable or not, always having regard to the protection of navigation where appropriate, should and do belong to the provinces themselves. That was proven, I think, by the fact that when the former premier of Ontario, Mr. Ferguson, made application to develop hydro-electric power on the international section of the St. Lawrence no objection was raised, and permission was given, although the project was never gone on with by the Ontario government. I might say further

and it was referred to by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail) this evening-that I believe it is true that had it not been for the contract made by the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario to take some 250,090 horse-power for a period of 40 years at $15 per horse-power,

Beauharnois-Mr. Gardiner

it would have 'been practically impossible for the Beauharnois corporation to float their bonds and continue their financing. I do regret that the power to be developed on the St. Lawrence river does not remain under public control, perhaps developed toy 'the provinces. However, as has been stated here by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Bell), while the people in the province of Ontario very largely believe in public ownership, the people in the province of Quebec are not of that opinion. They have a perfect right to believe in the benefits and the merits of private ownership as compared with those of public ownership.
I have stated that we were convinced that the water-power in this section of the river, being entirely within the province of Quebec, belonged to that province and that all the Dominion government had to do was make certain that in the development of the power derived from the 40,000 cubic foot diversion, navigation was safeguarded and not interfered with. Some reference was made this afternoon by one of the speakers to the fact that the abstraction of 40,000 cubic feet from the river did interfere with navigation, or at least that there was some doubt about it. I am not very clear on all the details of this transaction. I have not had time to look them up, to write them out or have somebody else write them out for me, but I am very firmly of the impression-and the former Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) bears me out in this- that the most capable engineers we could possibly secure said very definitely that the abstraction of the 40.000 cubic feet per second did not interfere with navigation on the St. Lawrence river. Therefore, assuming that the power did belong to the province; if it was also a matter of policy as far as the government was concerned that the water-power should go to the province-and I for one am in favour of that-further, if we were quite sure that navigation rights were protected, I was of the opinion and the government of the day was of the opinion that we had no moral right to refuse to sanction those plans. I never had any doubt as to whether the government had legal power to pass the order in council; as far as I am concerned I did not know the question had been raised. However, that is a legal question, and I do not see how even a committee can decide as to that. I should think it would be up to the courts to decide finally, though possibly in view of the reflections which have been made upon certain judges my hon. friend to my left will not even consent to have the courts decide it.
iMr. Euler.]
I am glad a committee is being appointed, although I believe the committee may have its difficulties. For instance, the Beauharnois corporation is a provincial company, and I have some doubt as to the jurisdiction of any committee of this house to investigate anything that is of provincial origin. However, it will be well to have the committee. I do not know how far it can go, but I trust that in making the reference to that committee my right hon. friend the Prime Minister will make it sufficiently broad and specific so that the Pharisaical accusations which have been made this afternoon will be cleared up, together with other points of law and of policy.

speechtext:
It is not necessary for
me to say very much in closing the debate, Mr. Speaker, since the Prime Minister has consented to the appointment of a committee of this house to investigate this whole matter With the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Euler) I also suggest to the Prime Minister that the reference to this committee be wide enough to include all matters which might come within the scope of such an inquiry.
The former Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) made a few statements during his address to which I think attention should be directed. In the first place, he was thoroughly convinced in his own mind that this water belonged to the province of Quebec. Then later on in his address he said he was not quite sure whether it belonged to Quebec or to the Dominion of Canada, because that matter was not definitely settled, so the latter part of his address was rather a contradiction of the first part. I am of the opinion that this matter should not be proceeded with until the rights of the provinces and of the Dominion are determined. I am also of the opinion that all this trouble would have been largely avoided if the Dominion government had resorted to the final court of appeal for a decision as to who owns the water in this river.
I will go further, Mr. Speaker; I will say that we in western Canada believe we have some rights in this river. We maintain, and I think we are right in maintaining, that this is not only an international river but a national river as well, in which all the people of Canada are interested, those of the maritime provinces as well as those of the west and

Grain Rates-Mr. Reid
central Canada. I maintain that before any such authority as this should have been given, the rights of the provinces and the Dominion should have been determined. This should have been done before the order in council was passed and work permitted to proceed; because after all is said and done the claims of the whole people of Canada are more important than the claims of the people of any province. The court of last resort should have been appealed to in order to determine this point.
The former Minister of Public Works quoted the Navigable Waters Protection Act, reading subsection (b) of section 2 and section 4. After he had read those sections he said, "Why, here is our authority to pass this order in council to divert water from the St. Lawrence." I will challenge any member of this house to show me any section in this act giving the government power to pass an order in council to divert water from a navigable stream. There is no such section in the act and there is no reference to that power being given any government. If the bill had come before parliament, this house would have had the right to permit the diversion of water from a navigable stream, but there is no question in my mind that the act gives no power to any government to permit that diversion by order in council.
This is one of the important points at issue, and it is a matter which should be inquired into. My hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Bell) made reference to certain companies which were contending with each other in the courts with regard to certain alleged wrongs done by one to another. I do not know very much about those matters; I have 'heard rumours, but I have not inquired into the merits of the claims of these companies. I am not interested in any company, whether it is the Beauhamois company or a company claiming damages from that company. I do not know anything about these companies beyond the odd references which 'have appeared in the press from time to time. I am not connected with any of them and am not interested in the success or failure of any of them. We have not raised the issue on that point, and we are not bringing up the matter on behalf of either of those companies. My hon. friend may rest assured that that is not the case as far as I am concerned.
I stated a few moments ago that I hoped the Prime Minister would make this reference wide enough to include all matters of importance in regard to this particular question. In order to obviate any possible recurrence of 22110-113i
what, has taken place in regard to the development of this particular section of the St Lawrence river, it should be the duty of the present government or any government which may be in power to have this matter referred to the court of last resort so that the people of Canada will know where they stand.
With the permission of the house I will withdraw my motion.
Motion (Mr. Gardiner) withdrawn. SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, I desire to discuss a question which I believe to be of urgent importance, namely the matter of domestic freight rates which are ai present affecting adversely the farmers of British Columbia, and before I sit down I intend to move an amendment to the motion to go into supply.
I realize that this question has been before the house many times, but I doubt very much whether the question of domestic freight rates was ever of more importance or presented graver possibilities to the poultrymea and those who keep dairy stock in the province of British Columbia than it is at the present time. It is not my intention to labour the question with a mass of statistical data, or unduly to delay the business of the house, but speaking on behalf of those in British Columbia who are dependent on the poultry and dairying industries for their livelihood, I must say that the time has long passed for the reduction of the present discriminatory domestic freight rate on grain and its products moving west to British Columbia. The matter. I say, is urgent; I believe it is important and serious enough to warrant the immediate attention of the government.
It is quite true that the question of railway rates has been discussed previously in this parliament and has been argued before the Board of Railway Commissioners in years past, but the fact remains that the poultry-men in British Columbia have never been in such dire straits as they have been during the past few months, and the same may be said of the farmers on the prairies who have their grain to sell. I intend to plead as best I can the case for these people in the sincere
Grain Rates-Mr. Reid

hope that the government will take speedy action to remedy what has been a long-standing grievance.
Since coming to Ottawa I have been surprised at the seeming lack of information on the part of many hon. members with regard to the position of British Columbia in her fight for a revision of the domestic freight rates. I intend to review the situation as briefly as possible and to show that the domestic freight rates to British Columbia from eastern points are discriminatory and unfair, not only in relation to export rates but as compared with the rates applicable to other sections of the Dominion. I believe I will be upheld in my argument by every fairminded member, because I do not think &ny hon. member will deny that the province of British Columbia is just as much entitled to equitable treatment in the matter of railway rates as is any other province in Canada. To my mind British Columbia since confederation has been treated more as an orphan than as a rightful and important member of the confederation. To obtain an intelligent view of our case it will be necessary to cite authorities dating from before confederation down to the time of our becoming a part of the Dominion in 1871.
One of the inducements offered to British Columbia, then a colony, to join the Dominion was a promise to construct a railway to establish speedy communication with other parts of the Dominion of Canada and at the same time to link up the Atlantic with the Pacific. To present the full facts it is necessary to go back to crown colony days. The preamble of the British North America Act of 1867 sets out that the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick desired to be united with a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom, and that such a union would conduce to the welfare of the provinces and of the British Empire. The dominating influence was that confederation was necessary to the empire as a whole, and provision was made for the admission of other parts of British North America into the union. It is the violation of this spirit of unity which has brought about the unjust conditions which we are now requesting should be removed. The inducement offered by the imperial govern-nent to British Columbia to join confedera-;ion is contained in the following quotation from the despatch of Earl Granville:
Most especially is this true in the case of internal transit. It is evident that the establishment of a British line of communication between the Atlantic and the Pacific oceans is far more feasible by the operation of a single government, responsible for the progress of both
[Mr. Reid.}
shores of the continent, than by a bargain negotiated between separate, perhaps in some respects rival, governments and legislatures.
The San Francisco of British North America would, under these circumstances, hold a greater commercial and political position than would be attainable by the capital of the isolated colony of British Columbia.
The proposed terms of the union which were drawn up read as follows:
Inasmuch as no real union can subsist between this colony and Canada without the speedy establishment of communication across the Rocky mountains by coach road and railway, the Dominion shall, within three years from date of union, construct and open for traffic such coach road from some point on the line of the main trunk road, and shall further engage to use all means in her power to complete such railway communication at the earliest practicable date, and that surveys to determine the proper line of such railway shall be at once commenced, and that a sum not less than one million dollars shall be expended in every year, from and after three years from date of union, in actually constructing the initial section of such railway from the seaboard of British Columbia to connect with the railway system of Canada.
Negotiations varied the proposed terms to some extent, but the dominant thought throughout was railway connection between the Atlantic and the Pacific. Section 11 of the terms of union agreed upon as a result of Earl Granville's despatch reads as follows:
The government of the Dominion undertake to secure the commencement simultaneously within two years from the date of union, of the construction of a railway from the Pacific towards the Rocky mountains, and from such point as may be selected, east of the Rocky mountains towards the Pacific, to connect the seaboard of British Columbia with the railway system of Canada; and. further to secure the completion of such railway within ten years from the date of union.
And the government of British Columbia agrees to convey to the Dominion government, in trust, to be appropriated in such manner as the Dominion government may deem advisable in furtherance of the construction of the said railway, a similar extent of public lands along the line of railway throughout its entire length in British Columbia, not to exceed, however, twenty (20) miles on each side of the said line.
It will be noticed that British Columbia was called upon to contribute a large grant of land in addition to her share of the other burdens put upon the nation by the construction of the transcontinental railway. In addition to this huge land grant British Columbia gave up many years before the railway was completed her customs tariff, which under the agreement she had the right to retain until the completion of the railway. An important fact which is not generally known is that the Dominion Railway Act, in

Grain Rates-Mr. Reid
force in 1871, made illegal any discrimination of toll. Subsection 6 of section 12, chapter
68, reads:
All or any of the tolls may by any by-law be reduced and again raised as often as necessary for the interests of the undertaking, but the same tolls shall be payable at the same time and under the same circumstances upon all goods by all persons or class of persons by any by-laws relating to tolls.
Some hon. members have said that they are not lawyers. I have made it clear that I am not a lawyer and I have no desire to be one, but I would say that no discrimination would have been possible under that section. In the Railway Act of 1879 the same proviso was included, providing against discrimination of tolls. However, we may differ as to that, the construction of the transcontinental railway was the dominant factor in inducing British Columbia to enter confederation, and I think I am stating a well founded belief when I say that had the people of British Columbia at that time known or been told that higher railway tolls would be exacted from her people than from the people of other parts of the Dominion, it is doubtful whether at that time she would have entered confederation and so become part of the Dominion of Canada.
The Dominion, as many hon. members know, entered into an agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to construct a line. It may be argued that the terms of union were not binding upon the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. When were any terms binding on the Canadian Pacific? The Canadian Pacific Railway Company certainly knew at that time that the Railway Act of 1868 did not allow them to discriminate as to freight tolls.
Regarding the construction of the first railway to the coast, it is not as well known as it should be that a route had been surveyed and laid out by the Dominion government over which the Canadian Pacific had contracted to build a railway to the Pacific coast. The Canadian Pacific did not adhere to that contract, and, instead, built the railway some 200 miles south of the proposed route and over the Rockies. Had the Canadian Pacific adhered to the route contracted for, there would not have been any mountain grades or mountain construction in British Columbia. As many hon. members know, the land in the Dominion of Canada slopes to the north, and the route which the Canadian Pacific abandoned as being no good is now the excellent route that was chosen by the Canadian National Railways and is now used by
their line from Vancouver to Edmonton, and which by the way is some 1,600 feet lower than the route chosen by the Canadian Pacific. If the Canadian Pacific had taken the Yellow-head pass route, the mountain differential in all probability would never have been put into effect. If, however, the Canadian Pacific blundered, and the parliament of Canada erred in permitting the change, that is no justifiable reason why British Columbia should be called upon to pay the whole cost of the error of the whole of Canada. The grades over the Canadian National railway route are nothing like those over the route used by the Canadian Pacific. It has sometimes been remarked: Look at what the Canadian Pacific has done for Canada. But having regard to the large subsidies paid by this country to the Canadian Pacific and the enormous grants made to them of the best of our lands, I think hon. members will agree with me when I say: Look at what this country has done for the Canadian Pacific. I am going to mention some of these subsidies. In cash the Canadian Pacific received $25,000,000; in constructed railways and services, another $38,000,000; in cash in exchange for subsidy lands, over $10,000,000, and a total of 18,000,000 acres of some of our best lands. In this way the Canadian Pacific easily received well over $110,000,000 from the Dominion of Canada.
The rate discrimination of the Canadian Pacific has always been resented by British Columbia. In 1906 and 1910 it was contested before the Board of Railway Commissioners, without result. Failure to obtain a removal of the discriminatory rates was one reason for the agreement of the Canadian National Railways to construct its line over the route originally contemplated by the Canadian Pacific, and this agreement was justified largely on the ground that such a road would reduce rates in that province and permit British Columbia to get into the consuming markets of the prairies on rates that were reasonable and just, and that the rates known as mountain scale rates would be eliminated.
In order to be certain that there would be no misunderstanding of what these new rates would be, the government of the day entered into another agreement intended to guarantee absolutely the promised reduction in railway rates. The agreement is contained in chapter 3 of the statutes of British Columbia, but at the moment I have not time to read the section dealing with it. The province at that time was very much alarmed regarding the rates, and was taking every precaution to see that there would be no further discrimination. The object of the then
Grain Rates-Mr. Reid

premier, Sir Richard McBride, in entering into the agreement, was not only to secure lower rates on the Canadian Pacific but also to force the general rates down to a reasonable point on any other transcontinental railway. British Columbia at that time was willing to guarantee $40,000,000 to another railway, so resentful did she feel over the Canadian Pacific. This, however, was going to place a competitor in the railway field, a factor which was not at all relished at the time by other private interests, and especially with the province of British Columbia backing those new railways to the limit. But, Mr. Speaker, I ask you to note what happened. The Dominion of Canada was, I believe, importuned to some extent, and passed an act in 1914 simply declaring the Canadian National Railways, to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, thus at one stroke taking the power of fixing rates out, of the hands of the province of British Columbia. I believe I am right when I say that the Canadian Pacific were the first to suggest such a line of action to the Dominion government. That is a brief history of the railways and railway companies of British Columbia since the day the province entered confederation, and I believe it should be more fully known that it is at present; for it is well, in my opinion, that these facts be had in mind before one proceeds with arguments as to the merits of our claim which are even more convincing.
I do not intend to make any extended argument in regard to freight rates generally, because, first, I do not wish to take up the time of the house in any general discussion, and, second, I want to keep to the main purpose of my address, which aims at this time only to bring about the necessary relief to the many purchasers and users of grain in British Columbia. The arguments from the point of view of the prairie farmers as sellers of grain can very well be left to hon. members from those districts. I intend, therefore, to confine my remarks to the discriminatory domestic	freight rate	which is	operativeagainst the province of British Columbia and which we in British Columbia are called upon to pay on all grain and its products purchased in Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba for domestic use. domestic use is 41i cents per 100 pounds. We claim not only that the rates on grain for domestic purposes are excessive, but that the rates on grain for export are much higher

through the port of Vancouver than they are to eastern points.
I contend that a domestic rate of 41i cents per 100 pounds as against 20 cents for export is both excessive and discriminatory and is acting as a real barrier to our progress and development. While I am aware that the principle advanced by the railway companies is that export and domestic rates on any particular commodity, being based on different conditions as to marketing, may properly differ in amount for the like per mile service, I affirm, however, that from all the arguments advanced or presented on behalf of the railway companies before the Board of Railway Commissioners, no statistical evidence has yet been given, so far as I am aware, to substantiate the rates charged on grain westbound to Vancouver by either the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian National.
British Columbia, as we all know, produces less wheat than any other province in proportion to her population, and so the question of rates on grain and flour for local consumption is of far greater importance to every section of her people than to those of any other province of Canada. We in British Columbia at least should have rates the same as the lowest accorded to any of the other provinces. From prairie points eastward to Fort William, there is no difference between the rates on grain and flour for export and those on grain and flour for domestic use. Why should there be such a difference to British Columbia? The population at the head of the lakes get the full benefit of an export rail rate on their domestic supplies, which are, by the way, not large enough to be considered as a factor in the case. In fact they are hauling grain for domestic purposes from points in Saskatchewan to Fort William or Port Arthur for as low as 19 cents as against 4JA cents per 100 pounds to British Columbia, although the distance is only half as great. In this way the greater part of the two larger provinces of the Dominion may receive the bulk of their domestic supplies of wheiat and flour at export rates.
Let us bear in mind also that the domestic rate which we pay is for inferior grades of wheat, not for No. 1 or No. 2 northern. Let us see just what some of these rates are. The all rail export rate from Fort William to Montreal is 34J cents per one hundred pounds. The domestic rate is 37 J cents, which is just three cents higher than the export rate. Mark this; the rail distance from Fort William to Montreal is 992 miles, which is greater by more than one-half than the distance from

Calgary to Vancouver, which is only 642 miles on the Canadian Pacific railway. In the face of those figures, surely British Columbia is entitled to some fairer treatment than she now receives at the hands of the railway companies. A domestic rate of three cents over the export rate from prairie points to Vancouver would represent the same difference between domestic and export rates as now prevails on the all rail grain movement from Fort William to Montreal. But it would not put us in the same favoured position as Montreal, because central Canada generally, including Montreal, gets the bulk of its domestic supplies at export rates.
The argument is generally put forward that the reason the rates on grain and flour are much higher westbound than eastbound is found in the so-called physical difficulties in getting into British Columbia. I would point out, Mr. Speaker-and I believe it is important information which should be more fully and generally known-that according to evidence submitted before the Board of Railway Commissioners in 1926, not only were the construction costs greater in some of the other provinces than in British Columbia, but the cost of maintenance is less in British Columbia than in many of the other provinces. The wrong impression in this respect which has prevailed for a considerable time should be corrected, and in my opinion now is the time to make the correction.
I am going to give a few instances as to the cost of construction at other points in Canada as compared to the cost through the Rockies. From Kamloops to Hope, 168 miles, cost 8133,563 per mile; eastern Canada, Montreal to Ottawa, 111 miles, cost 8178,614 per mile; British Columbia, Hope to Fraser River junction, 77 miles, cost $51,544 per mile; eastern Canada, Joliette to Gameau Junction, 61-49 miles, cost $62,394 per mile; British Columbia, Fraser River Junction to Grandview, Manitoba, 1,381 miles, cost $55,572 per mile; Montreal to Winnipeg, 1,451 miles, cost $59,313 per mile.
With regard to the cost of operation, the Canadian Pacific Railway have submitted a statement, which can be found at page 142 of the report of the Board of Railway Commissioners for the year 1925, setting out the operating cost per gross ton mile throughout its system by districts.
The Canadian National Railway shows that the operating costs in 1925 per mile of road in British Columbia were $3,825.50, and in the prairie districts, $4,707.34 per mile. In British Columbia the operating expenses were
shown to be about the same as in Ontario, and less than in Quebec and New Brunswick.
It is perfectly clear to me, Mr. Speaker, that unless the rates are adjusted to allow all traffic to move more freely, and with the proper degree of freedom between the prairies and the Pacific coast, the purpose of the construction of the Canadian National railway to Vancouver will not have been achieved and the money paid by the Dominion treasury to secure its construction will in a large measure have been thrown away.
I have endeavoured to place before the house important and general statistical facts, such as:
1.	The conditions under which British Columbia entered confederation.
2.	The conditions under which British Columbia was asked to enter the Dominion of Canada, and the inducements offered to her, which were rail connections with the Atlantic.
3.	The large grants of land which British Columbia gave for the building of the railway.
4.	The fact that the Railway Act of that day prohibited the imposition of discriminatory tolls.
5.	The varying' of the act of 1868 so as to permit an inequality of treatment, being a direct violation of the spirit of the terms of union.
6.	The fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company changed the excellent route laid down for them by the Dominion and chose for themselves a more difficult route, because it was shorter by some 130 miles.
7.	The fact that the Dominion government took away from the province of British Columbia the right British Columbia had, up, to that time to fix and control the rates and tolls of the Canadian Northern Pacific by simply declaring the work to be for the general benefit of Canada.
8.	I have also given figures which have been sworn to before the Board of Railway Commissioners, proving that the cost of construction was greater in some of the eastern provinces than from Alberta to British Columbia, and
9.	Figures submitted by both the Canadian Pacific Railway and Canadian National Railways showing that operating costs were less in British Columbia than in many other provinces in the east, and
10.	The pusher mileage is also less in British Columbia.
